Updated 5/15/26

# The Ultimate Guide to Math Websites: Khan Academy, Prodigy, IXL & More

The best math websites for kids right now:

* **[Khan Academy](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/khan-academy-website)** – Free, comprehensive, with AI tutoring (Khanmigo)
* **[Prodigy](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/prodigy-website)** – RPG-style math practice that kids actually ask to do
* **[IXL](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/ixl-website)** – Adaptive curriculum with detailed analytics (subscription required)
* **[Coolmath Games](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/coolmath-games-website)** – Logic puzzles disguised as fun
* **[Desmos](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/desmos-website)** – Visual graphing calculator for older kids

Looking at our Screenwise community data, **45% of families are using laptops for learning**, while **50% report unsupervised tablet use**. The average kid is getting about **4.2 hours of screen time daily**—so if some of that's going to happen anyway, math practice sites are one of the better ways to spend it.

## Screenwise Parents

[See all](/videos)

Why This Matters

Math anxiety is real, and it often starts when kids fall behind and can't catch up in a classroom moving at one pace for 25+ students. The right math website can let your child work at their own speed, fill gaps without shame, and—this is key—actually enjoy the process.

But here's the thing: not all math sites are created equal. Some are glorified worksheets with cartoon mascots. Others are so gamified that kids forget they're learning anything. And a few genuinely balance engagement with rigor.

The platforms below have been vetted by millions of families, backed by research showing measurable gains, and—most importantly—they give **you** visibility into what your kid is actually learning.

[Khan Academy](https://www.khanacademy.org/?source=screenwisedotapp&utm=screenwise)

**Best for:** K-12, comprehensive learning, filling gaps  
 **Cost:** Free (seriously, completely free)  
 **Ages:** 2-18+

[Khan Academy](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/khan-academy-website) remains the gold standard for free math education in 2026. The library of video lessons and practice problems is created by expert educators and aligned to state standards, covering everything from counting to calculus.

What makes Khan Academy special is its **mastery-based progression**—kids can't move forward until they've demonstrated understanding, which prevents those knowledge gaps that compound over time. The platform tracks every skill, so you can see exactly where your child is thriving and where they're stuck.

**New in 2024-2025:** The AI-powered tutor **Khanmigo** (built on GPT-4) offers personalized hints and step-by-step explanations. Instead of just giving answers, it asks guiding questions—think Socratic method, but patient and available 24/7. This is a game-changer for kids who need help but don't want to ask in class.

**Parent dashboard** shows completed skills, time spent, and mastery levels. You can set goals, assign specific content, and actually see if that "I'm doing Khan Academy!" claim is homework or just YouTube in another tab.

For younger kids (ages 2-8), there's **[Khan Academy Kids](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/khan-academy-kids-app)**—a separate app with story-based lessons, games, and songs that build early math foundations. Also completely free.

**Bottom line:** If you're only going to use one math resource, make it Khan Academy. It's free, it's comprehensive, and it actually works.

[Prodigy](https://www.prodigygame.com/main-en?source=screenwisedotapp&utm=screenwise)

**Best for:** Making practice feel like play  
 **Cost:** Free for basic, paid memberships unlock extras  
 **Ages:** 6-14 (grades 1-8)

[Prodigy](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/prodigy-website) turns math practice into a full RPG adventure. Kids create wizard avatars, explore fantasy worlds, battle monsters, and complete quests—all by solving standards-aligned math problems. It's the rare edutainment platform that kids genuinely beg to use.

The engagement numbers back this up: **91% of surveyed parents say their children enjoy using Prodigy**. Teachers report measurable gains too—some see a **45% increase in standardized test scores** after daily 25-minute sessions.

The platform adapts to your child's level, serving up problems that challenge without overwhelming. It also now includes English language arts content alongside math.

**Parent/teacher dashboard** provides detailed reports on skill growth, time spent, and areas needing work. You can see which specific standards your child has mastered and where they need more practice.

**The catch:** The free version is fully functional for learning, but paid memberships ($9.95-14.95/month) unlock cosmetic items, pets, and extra game content. This can create some "but everyone else has a membership!" pressure, especially in classrooms where Prodigy is assigned. Teachers get the platform free, which is why it's so common in schools.

**Real talk:** The gamification works, but it also means kids are motivated by leveling up their character, not necessarily by understanding fractions. That's fine—motivation is motivation—but don't expect deep mathematical reasoning. This is practice, not conceptual learning.

[IXL](https://www.ixl.com/?source=screenwisedotapp&utm=screenwise)

**Best for:** Comprehensive curriculum, detailed analytics  
 **Cost:** $9.95/month (one subject) to $19.95/month (all subjects)  
 **Ages:** Pre-K through 12th grade

[IXL](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/ixl-website) is the powerhouse platform serving **over 17 million students** who have collectively answered **more than 160 billion questions**. It covers math, language arts, science, social studies, and Spanish with an adaptive engine that adjusts difficulty in real-time.

The platform emphasizes **mastery through practice**—lots and lots of practice. Each skill has unlimited questions, and the system tracks performance with a "SmartScore" that shows progress toward mastery (100 means mastery, and it takes consistent correct answers to get there).

**Real-time diagnostics** show exactly where your child stands on each skill, with personalized recommendations for what to work on next. The analytics are incredibly detailed—you can see how long they spent, which questions they missed, and how their performance compares to grade-level expectations.

**The awards and certificates system** keeps kids motivated, and the "immersive learning experience" uses visual and interactive elements to make abstract concepts concrete.

**The downside:** IXL requires a paid subscription (unlike Khan Academy), and some kids find the interface less engaging than game-based platforms like Prodigy. The focus on drill-and-practice can also feel tedious for kids who prefer more creative or exploratory learning.

**Best use case:** Families who want comprehensive coverage across multiple subjects with granular tracking. If you're homeschooling or supplementing school with serious remediation, IXL's depth is hard to beat.

[Coolmath Games](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/coolmath-games-website)

**Best for:** Logic, problem-solving, spatial reasoning  
 **Cost:** Free (ad-supported)  
 **Ages:** 8+

[Coolmath Games](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/coolmath-games-website) is the site that's been unblocked in school computer labs since 2008. It's technically a "math" site, but really it's a collection of logic puzzles, strategy games, and brain teasers that build mathematical thinking without feeling like homework.

Games like *Run 3*, *Papa's Freezeria*, and *Fireboy and Watergirl* teach spatial reasoning, pattern recognition, and problem-solving. There's no curriculum alignment, no progress tracking for parents, and no explicit "learn fractions" goals—but kids are building the cognitive skills that underpin math success.

**Real talk:** This is where kids go when they finish their "real" work. And that's fine! The games are genuinely fun, and they're training brains to think logically. Just don't expect it to replace actual math practice.

[Desmos](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/desmos-website)

**Best for:** Visualizing algebra, geometry, and data  
 **Cost:** Free  
 **Ages:** 10+ (middle school and up)

[Desmos](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/desmos-website) is the interactive graphing calculator that makes math visual. Kids can type in equations and instantly see the graphs, manipulate variables with sliders, and explore how functions behave.

It's especially powerful for **algebra and pre-calculus**, where being able to *see* what a function does makes abstract concepts click. Teachers love it because it's free and browser-based (no downloads, no accounts required for basic use).

There are also pre-built activities and lessons that guide students through concepts with interactive explorations. Think "what happens to the graph when you change the coefficient?" type investigations.

**Parent note:** This isn't a practice platform—it's a tool. Your kid won't spend hours on Desmos like they might on Prodigy. But when they're stuck on graphing or need to visualize a concept, it's invaluable.

Honorable Mentions

* **[Math Playground](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/math-playground-website)** – Free site with games and logic puzzles for elementary and middle school
* **[Zearn](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/zearn-website)** – Free, standards-aligned lessons with a focus on conceptual understanding (often used in schools)
* **[Matific](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/matific-website)** – Game-based learning for K-6, subscription required
* **[SplashLearn](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/splashlearn-website)** – Pre-K to 5th grade, game-based, subscription required

Age-Appropriate Guidance

**Ages 5-8 (K-2nd grade):**  
 Start with **[Khan Academy Kids](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/khan-academy-kids-app)** for foundational skills in a playful, story-based format. Add **[Prodigy](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/prodigy-website)** if they're ready for more structured practice.

**Ages 8-11 (3rd-5th grade):**  
 **[Khan Academy](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/khan-academy-website)** for comprehensive learning, **[Prodigy](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/prodigy-website)** for daily practice, **[Coolmath Games](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/coolmath-games-website)** for logic and fun.

**Ages 11-14 (6th-8th grade):**  
 **[Khan Academy](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/khan-academy-website)** remains essential, add **[Desmos](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/desmos-website)** for visualizing algebra. **[IXL](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/ixl-website)** if you want detailed tracking across subjects.

**Ages 14+ (high school):**  
 **[Khan Academy](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/khan-academy-website)** for everything from Algebra 2 through AP Calculus, **[Desmos](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/desmos-website)** for graphing and exploration.

What Parents Should Know

**1. Free doesn't mean worse.**  
 Khan Academy is completely free and arguably the best resource available. Don't feel like you need to pay for a subscription unless you want the specific features (like IXL's detailed analytics or Prodigy's game extras).

**2. These aren't magic bullets.**  
 Even the best platform won't help if your kid is clicking through without thinking. The goal is understanding, not completion. Check in on what they're learning, not just that they spent 30 minutes on the site.

**3. Gamification is a tool, not a solution.**  
 Prodigy's RPG format gets kids to practice, but make sure they're connecting the math to real understanding. If they can't explain *why* an answer is correct, the game isn't doing its job.

**4. Use the parent dashboards.**  
 Every major platform has analytics for a reason. Spend 5 minutes a week reviewing what your child worked on, where they're struggling, and where they're excelling. That visibility is the real superpower of these tools.

**5. Mix it up.**  
 No single platform does everything. Khan Academy for instruction and conceptual learning, Prodigy for daily practice, Desmos for visualization, Coolmath for fun. Different tools for different needs.

The Bottom Line

The best math website for your family depends on your goals:

* **Need free and comprehensive?** [Khan Academy](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/khan-academy-website) all the way.
* **Want kids to actually enjoy practice?** [Prodigy](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/prodigy-website) delivers.
* **Need detailed tracking and multi-subject support?** [IXL](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/ixl-website) is worth the subscription.
* **Just want to sneak in some logic skills?** [Coolmath Games](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/coolmath-games-website) has you covered.

With **45% of families in our community using laptops for learning** and screen time averaging over 4 hours a day, these platforms are a way to make some of that time genuinely productive. The key is picking tools that fit your child's learning style, using the parent dashboards to stay informed, and remembering that these are supplements—not replacements—for real math instruction.

Start with one platform, give it two weeks, and see if it sticks. If your kid is asking to do more math, you've found the right fit.

Next Steps

1. **Try Khan Academy first** (it's free, comprehensive, and works for all ages)
2. **Set up parent accounts** on whatever platforms you choose so you can track progress
3. **Start small**—15-20 minutes a day is plenty
4. **Check in weekly** to see what they're learning and where they need help
5. **Mix in fun**—[Coolmath Games](https://screenwiseapp.com/media/coolmath-games-website) or [logic puzzles](https://screenwiseapp.com/guides/logic-puzzles-for-kids) keep math feeling playful

Want to explore more ways to make learning engaging? Check out our guides on [coding websites for kids](https://screenwiseapp.com/guides/coding-websites-for-kids), [educational YouTube channels](https://screenwiseapp.com/guides/educational-youtube-channels), and [screen time that actually builds skills](https://screenwiseapp.com/guides/productive-screen-time-for-kids).

# IXL vs Khan Academy: Which One Closes Skill Gaps Faster

IXL runs on a paid, adaptive-drill model. Khan Academy doesn't charge a cent for its video courses. Compare both before you settle on one.

Last updated: Aug 20, 2026

Read time: 10 min

![IXL app icon on an orange background compared side by side with the Khan Academy app icon on a teal background, illustrating an IXL vs Khan Academy learning platform comparison](https://a.storyblok.com/f/289689962598839/1200x660/b8388fc3dd/ixl-app-icon-on-an-orange-background-compared-side-by-side-with-the-khan-academy-app-icon-on-a-teal-background-illustrating-an-ixl-vs-khan-academy-learning-platform-comparison.webp/m/3840x0/filters:quality(75))

![Kateryna Zabigailo](https://a.storyblok.com/f/289689962598839/886x886/6a68c5d3a2/kateryna.webp/m/3840x0/filters:quality(75))

ByKateryna Zabigailo

Head of Product Marketing at Nibble

Are you stuck on the same math skill for weeks? That frustration usually leads straight to the IXL vs Khan Academy question. Khan Academy runs on free video lessons. IXL charges for adaptive practice. Each one gets a student from confused to confident by a different route, and price is only part of the story.

A peer-reviewed study in [PNAS](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2507708123) tracked roughly 200,000 students across hundreds of school districts and found that more time spent practicing on Khan Academy lined up with real gains on state math tests.

For a student, either platform can close a real skill gap with steady use. Both are built with younger learners in mind. Nibble takes a different angle, it's designed for adults who want their own short daily lesson, separate from what their kids are working through.

Try the [Nibble app](https://nibble-app.com/funnels/general-en?utm_source=organic_website&utm_section=blogpage&utm_slug=ixl-vs-khan-academy) for five minutes while your kid works through their next lesson.

## Quick summary: IXL vs Khan Academy in 30 seconds

A fast look at how the two platforms stack up before the full breakdown below.

* IXL charges a monthly subscription, while Khan Academy stays free for every core course.
* Adaptive practice questions and the SmartScore system make up the core of IXL's approach.
* Video lessons and full course sequences, including AP classes and SAT prep, anchor Khan Academy.
* Parents get skill-level progress reports through IXL's dashboard, broken down by individual standard.
* Self-directed learners tend to do well with Khan Academy's mastery-based course structure.

Keep reading for the breakdown: current pricing, honest pros and cons for each platform, and the gap neither one covers.

## What IXL and Khan Academy each teach

Each platform builds its curriculum around a different core idea.

### What IXL covers

**IXL** is a subscription practice platform built around adaptive questions, covering math, ELA, science, social studies, and Spanish. Each question adjusts based on how a student answers.

IXL Learning built its SmartScore system to track mastery skill by skill instead of subject by subject. The platform spans grade levels from Pre-K through 12th grade, so a family can stay on one account as a kid moves up through school.

### What Khan Academy covers

**Khan Academy** leans on free video lessons, spanning a nonprofit K-12 library that stretches into early college courses. A student watches a short lesson, then works through practice problems tied to it.

Its AI study tool, Khanmigo, uses Socratic-style prompts rather than handing over an answer outright. Khan Academy's catalog stretches from arithmetic to multivariable calculus, as our [Khan Academy review](https://nibble-app.com/blog/khan-academy-review) covers in more detail.

Beyond math, the library covers science, computer programming, art history, economics, and grammar, which makes it a reasonable stop for a student studying for more than one subject at once.

📚 **Lessons mix text, video, audio, and quick games, so nothing feels like one long study session. Try the** [**Nibble app**](https://nibble-app.com/funnels/general-en?utm_source=organic_website&utm_section=blogpage&utm_slug=ixl-vs-khan-academy) **and switch formats whenever you want.**

## Adaptive drills vs free video lessons

Each platform built a very different practice engine.

### How IXL practice works

IXL runs on a practice-question engine. Its Real-Time Diagnostic places a new student at their true grade level before any skill work begins.

A student answers, gets immediate feedback, and the difficulty shifts right away. IXL goes deeper on individual state standards, covering science, social studies, and language arts along the way.

### How Khan Academy practice works

Video lessons anchor Khan Academy's side of this comparison, paired with guided practice sets and mastery points that unlock the next unit.

Khan Academy goes deeper on full linear courses, like AP Calculus or US History, with hint videos built into its feedback.

| Feature | IXL | Khan Academy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subjects covered | Math, ELA, science, social studies, Spanish | Math, science, ELA, social studies, test prep, early college |
| Practice format | Adaptive practice questions with SmartScore | Guided practice sets tied to video lessons |
| Feedback | Immediate feedback on every question | Immediate feedback plus hint videos |
| Progress tracking | Skill analytics, Real-Time Diagnostic, parent dashboard | Mastery points, progress reports by unit |
| Teacher tools | Assignment builder, state standards alignment | Class codes, assignable playlists, Khanmigo AI study tool |
| Cost | Paid subscription | Free (Khanmigo add-on costs extra) |

[Brainscape](https://nibble-app.com/blog/brainscape) leans on flashcards and active recall instead of a live score, which suits a different kind of learner than either platform here.

📚 **Nibble tracks a daily streak instead of a mastery score, with no pressure to hit 100 percent on anything. Get** [**Nibble**](https://nibble-app.com/funnels/general-en?utm_source=organic_website&utm_section=blogpage&utm_slug=ixl-vs-khan-academy) **and start your own streak today.**

## Classroom setup: Google Classroom, class codes, and rosters

Teachers who already run a classroom on Google Classroom, Schoology, or Canvas will find both platforms fit into that setup, just in different ways.

**IXL's classroom setup:**

1. Import a full roster from Google Classroom in a few clicks, with auto-sync going forward.
2. Share any skill straight to Google Classroom and attach a SmartScore goal as the point value.
3. Connect through Schoology, Canvas, or Clever for single sign-on across the class.
4. Pull Real-Time Diagnostic results without ever leaving the LMS.

**Khan Academy's classroom setup:**

1. Build a class manually or import one directly from Google Classroom.
2. Let students join with a class code instead of a full roster import.
3. Use Khanmigo Teacher Tools for lesson hooks and IEP accommodations from the same dashboard.
4. Practice through a mobile app, so a student isn't tied to a desktop.

Content assigned inside Google Classroom doesn't automatically report back to Khan Academy's own teacher dashboard, which trips up plenty of teachers. Assigning it in both places is usually the only way to see complete progress data.

## Pricing breakdown: What you'll pay each month

The two platforms stack up very differently on cost.

### IXL pricing

IXL's Single subject plan runs $9.95 a month for either Math (Pre-K to Calculus) or Language Arts (Pre-K to 12). The Combo package covers both of those subjects for $15.95 a month.

The Core subjects plan costs $19.95 a month and adds Science (K to Physics) and Social Studies (K to 12) on top of Math and Language Arts.

Annual billing runs $79, $129, or $159 across those three tiers, with each extra child adding $4 a month or $40 a year.

That price gap is why some families compare IXL to cheaper drill-based options like Kumon worksheets. Classroom licenses start at $299 a year for a group of 25 students on one subject.

### Khan Academy pricing

Khan Academy's core courses stay free forever for students, teachers, and independent learners. Khanmigo, its AI tutor, costs $4 a month or $44 a year for a parent account.

Teachers get Khanmigo free after a quick verification step. Schools and districts under 1,000 seats can add it through an Enterprise Starter plan, priced at $10 per student a year.

Looked at over a full year, the gap between the two platforms adds up fast. A family paying for IXL's Core subjects plan spends close to $240 a year, while a family sticking with Khan Academy's free core courses spends nothing beyond an optional Khanmigo add-on.

| Teacher | Included with a school or classroom license | Free, including Khanmigo after a quick verification step |

## Where IXL's SmartScore system helps and hurts

IXL earns real praise for its depth, useful for remediation and enrichment alike, but it isn't without friction for some kids.

**IXL pros:**

* Granular skill analytics that show exactly where skill gaps show up, down to a single standard.
* Strong alignment with state standards, which suits test prep and remediation work.
* A detailed parent dashboard with progress reports broken down by subject and skill.
* Spanish is part of IXL's subject range too, a depth few competitors match.

**IXL cons:**

* Cost adds up fast once a second kid or a second subject joins the plan, especially next to free alternatives.
* The drill-style format can feel repetitive for a kid who needs more variety to stay engaged.
* Some students find the interface less engaging than video-first platforms.

If a child needs more visual math practice than IXL's question format gives, [GeoGebra](https://nibble-app.com/blog/geogebra) offers hands-on geometry and algebra tools outside any subscription.

## Khan Academy's free access comes with a few trade-offs

Khan Academy earns praise for being free and thorough, though it asks more of a student who needs extra structure.

**Khan Academy pros:**

* Free access to nearly the entire K-12 curriculum, plus AP courses and SAT prep.
* Strong video instruction that walks through a concept step by step before practice starts.
* A nonprofit mission with no ads and no upsells cluttering the experience.
* Solid support for self-directed learners who want to move at their own pace.

Its SAT prep also runs through an official partnership with the College Board, lining practice questions up with the real exam.

**Khan Academy cons:**

* Less granular skill-by-skill diagnostics than IXL's SmartScore system.
* Practice sets can feel less adaptive question to question compared to IXL's engine.
* A younger kid may need more parent involvement to stay on task without a set curriculum path.

If a teenager wants to learn to code on their own time, [Sololearn](https://nibble-app.com/blog/sololearn) offers a similar self-directed structure outside Khan Academy's computer science courses.

## Choosing the right fit for your child's grade and style

Grade level and personality matter more than either platform's marketing lets on.

A younger kid usually does better with Khan Academy's video-first structure, which walks through a concept before any practice begins. An older student who already gets the concept but needs to close one gap for a state test tends to move faster through IXL's targeted questions.

Test prep splits along similar lines. Khan Academy's College Board partnership helps more with the SAT or an AP exam, while IXL's standards-aligned practice fits a specific state assessment better.

Cost tips the scale for a family juggling more than one kid or subject. Starting with Khan Academy's free core courses, then adding an IXL subscription only where a real skill gap shows up, keeps the bill down without giving up the diagnostics.

Not every student needs the same amount of structure, either. A self-directed kid can work through Khan Academy's courses with little oversight, but a kid who needs a short, scored session and a clear finish line usually does better with IXL.

## FAQs about IXL and Khan Academy

### Can I use IXL and Khan Academy together?

Yes, a lot of families do both at once. IXL tends to handle the day-to-day skill drilling and closing a specific gap, while Khan Academy covers the bigger picture: full courses, test prep, the works. They aren't stepping on each other's toes, so there's nothing to untangle if you use both.

### Should I pick IXL or Khan Academy for math specifically?

Honestly, it comes down to what's stuck. If your child gets the concept but keeps missing a specific type of problem, IXL's SmartScore drills usually close that gap fast. If the concept itself is the problem, sit them in front of a Khan Academy video first. Plenty of families end up using both.

### Is IXL or Khan Academy better for homeschooling?

Both work well for homeschooling, though for different reasons. IXL gives you a full curriculum with built-in progress tracking that many parents use as a record-keeping tool. Khan Academy adds more depth in full course sequences, like AP subjects, at no cost. Many homeschool families use Khan Academy as the core and add IXL for extra practice.

### Is Khan Academy really free for my family?

Yes, you get free access to Khan Academy's core courses, video lessons, and practice problems as an individual user. Khanmigo, its AI tutor, costs $4 a month or $44 a year if you want that add-on. Outside of Khanmigo, you won't hit a subscription fee anywhere on the main curriculum.

You'll pay $9.95 a month for one subject, $15.95 for a math and language arts combo, or $19.95 for all four core subjects. Each additional child on your plan costs $4 more a month. Annual billing brings the cost down for a full school year.

### Is it easy to cancel IXL if it's not working out?

Yes, and it's simple: cancel from your account settings whenever you want, and you keep access until your billing period wraps up. You don't need to worry about it, but it's worth noticing. IXL and Khan Academy track your child's progress in detail, and neither one is built with you in mind. An app built for adults, like Nibble, fills that gap without asking for a grade level.

## Abstract

Evaluating online educational platforms requires studying the design, development, and implementation of the learning environment as well as the learning materials, learners, and learning process to facilitate improvements in teaching and skill acquisition. The accelerated growth of online educational tools has prompted a need for systematic evaluation of online educational platforms. Khan Academy has experienced immense popularity and is used by students worldwide. However, little research has been conducted on the effects of Khan Academy at the individual level. Thus, the purpose of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of Khan Academy in teaching elementary math to three participants using objective methods. Participants completed worksheets prior to and following Khan Academy to determine its effectiveness in teaching targeted math skills. Results indicated that Khan Academy was effective for all three participants. Thus, Khan Academy may be an effective tool for acquisition of elementary math.

The COVID-19 pandemic emphasized the need for the systematic evaluation of online educational tools to understand their strengths and weaknesses. The pandemic affected students as well as educators, requiring them to adapt quickly to remote learning through online learning platforms (Hoofman & Secord, [2021](#CR12)). Online learning platforms varied from educational content that could be accessed at the student’s discretion to real-time lessons conducted by teachers using virtual meeting platforms (Schleicher, [2020](#CR31)). In addition to changes in instructional techniques, the pandemic also adversely affected the academic growth of students which became evident in the performance of students in math and reading (Hoofman & Secord, [2021](#CR12)). In 2022, the National Center for Education Statistics administered the National Assessment of Educational Progress’ (NAEP) long-term trend assessment to 9-year-old children to evaluate performance in math and reading (The Nation’s Report Card, [n.d.](#CR39)). Both math and reading scores decreased, which represented the first decrease in math scores and the largest decrease in reading scores since 1990. Given the rise of online learning platforms and decreases in academic performance, researchers (e.g., Vlachopoulos, [2020](#CR42)) have suggested the importance of evaluating and monitoring online learning platforms to assess their effects on student learning outcomes and experiences to improve online learning platforms.

Among the vast array of online learning platforms available (e.g., IXL, Zearn, MathXL, Dreambox), Khan Academy is popular. Khan Academy is visited by 20 million individuals per month, has more than 120 million registered users, is used in more than 190 countries, and has partnered with more than 200 school districts across the United States (Khan, [2021](#CR18)). The online learning platform has been featured on *60 Minutes*, TED, *John Stossel Documentary*, Public Broadcasting Service, *The Early Show*, CNN, Tom Brokaw, and *Piers Morgan Tonight* (Noer, [2012](#CR25)). Salman Khan created Khan Academy in 2008 as a nonprofit organization. Khan Academy provides a free and innovative online learning platform for learners ranging from pre-kindergarten to college, enabling millions of users to remotely access the contents offered in different disciplines (Vidergor & Ben-Amram, [2020](#CR41)) such as basic arithmetic, algebra, the Electoral College, and the French Revolution (Khan, [2006](#CR17)). The founder recommended teachers use Khan Academy for instruction to allow for more engaging activities during class such as collaborative projects (Khan, 2020). In fact, several studies suggest the efficacy of the components of Khan Academy such as the video tutorials when used in this manner (e.g., Light & Pierson, [2014](#CR20); Weeraratne & Chin, [2018](#CR44)).

Khan Academy has many benefits as compared to traditional, teacher-centered instruction. Teacher-centered instruction is often characterized as lecture-based pedagogy with minimal opportunities for students to interact with one another or apply the content during active-learning opportunities (Dimitrios et al., [2013](#CR6); Murphy et al., [2021](#CR24); Renau, [2016](#CR27)). Teacher-centered instruction might also include videos and the use of quizzes to increase the likelihood of students interacting with the class material. In a typical classroom, the student’s role is more passive (e.g., Serin, [2018](#CR32)), especially in comparison to student-directed learning environments. Khan Academy allows students more opportunities for active learning because it is a student-directed approach. Through assessment, Khan Academy identifies skill deficits. From identified deficits, lessons are individually identified which provide instructions in video format with corresponding practice problems (Khan, [2006](#CR17)). Given individual differences (e.g., learning histories) can affect the learning process, it is possible Khan Academy’s more individualized style of learning would benefit some learners (Jonassen & Grabowski, [1993](#CR13)).

According to Light and Pierson ([2014](#CR20)), there are three main components of Khan Academy. First, there are videos in which the Khan Academy instructor uses a simulated blackboard to teach using instructions and demonstrations. Second, the learner practices the skill using a bank of practice problems dynamically generated such that learners work on a variety of problems. If a learner makes an error during the practice problem, then the learner is given a choice of either watching the instructional video again or accessing hints, which are systematic, step-by-step textual explanations of how the problem should be solved. Following completion of the problem, the learner is provided with praise (e.g., “Nice work! Keep it up for 2 more.” with corresponding streamers and noise) or a prompt to complete the problem again (e.g., “Give it another shot! Try again, get help, or skip for now.”). Third, Khan Academy provides real time progress data, recording a learner’s activity, date of completion, level of proficiency, change, number of correct problems within a practice set, and time in minutes. In addition, teachers can access data in real time or in an accumulated format for an individual or a group of students.

There are other aspects of Khan Academy that may contribute to its effectiveness including the use of badges, energy points, avatars, and challenge patches (Khan, [2021](#CR18)). In general, Khan Academy allows each learner to structure the pace at which they learn and how they learn by providing them options to watch videos to understand the content, solve problem sets, and access additional videos or problem sets for advance learning without worrying about holding their peers or teachers back (Thompson, [2011](#CR40)). Although not explicitly stated, Khan Academy appears to align well with the behavior analytic teaching and instructional literatures including the use of (1) a curriculum that increases in difficulty as the learner acquires skills; (2) repeated practice; (3) prompts; (4) immediate feedback and reinforcement; and (5) progress monitoring (Chard et al., [2002](#CR4); Martens & Witt, [2004](#CR21); Skinner, [1954](#CR35)). In addition, Khan Academy’s personalized learning system may result in more effective learning than traditional instruction for individuals as Khan Academy assesses and programs for learner skill deficits, allowing for greater skill acquisition (Khan, [2021](#CR18)). In fact, Khan Academy may be similar to Fred Keller’s personalized system of instruction (PSI; Keller, [1968](#CR14)). PSI is self-paced instruction during which the learner is provided content in smaller units that become accessible to the learner progressively as they master each unit (Eyre, [2007](#CR7)). Khan Academy encompasses the elements of Keller’s PSI by providing learning instructions in the form of videos as well as text, dividing complicated concepts into small units that build as the learner progresses and acquires skills, and providing the learner with complete control on the pace of learning.

Khan Academy, as an effective learning platform for math, has been showcased in several studies (e.g., Khan, [2021](#CR18); Light & Pierson, [2014](#CR20); Weeraratne & Chin, [2018](#CR44)) and across a variety of ages, languages, cultures, and socioeconomic backgrounds (e.g., Light & Pierson, [2014](#CR20); Weeraratne & Chin, [2018](#CR44)). Although results support the effectiveness and preferred use of Khan Academy, the bulk of research is not peer reviewed (i.e., dissertation or thesis; e.g., Adams, [2016](#CR1); Kelly, [2018](#CR15); Kreller, [2022](#CR19); Reed, [2019](#CR26); Rossel, [2015](#CR29)) and uses descriptive methods (e.g., interviews, such as Vidergor & Ben-Amram, [2020](#CR41)), observational measures (e.g., Light & Pierson, [2014](#CR20)), or group research designs (e.g., Kelly & Rutherford, [2017](#CR16); Weeraratne & Chin, [2018](#CR44)). For example, Vidergor and Ben-Amram ([2020](#CR41)) examined the effectiveness of Khan Academy from a student’s perspective by conducting interviews and collecting self-report data in the form of reflective diaries. They concluded Khan Academy promoted independence and made the topic more interesting for the student. Although this study was beneficial in understanding the acceptability of Khan Academy for students, self-reporting as a method of data collection can be inaccurate or biased, threatening the validity and reliability of measurement (Critchfield & Perone, [1990](#CR5)). In addition, it is unclear how student performance was affected given the lack of objective performance measures.

Light and Pierson ([2014](#CR20)) conducted an observational study with five schools in Santiago, Chile, where teachers used Khan Academy to document the teachers’ implementation of Khan Academy and the resulting outcomes for the students. The researchers conducted interviews with students, teachers, and school administrators to understand their experiences with Khan Academy; focus groups with students; and observations. They observed a total of 25 math lessons taught with and without Khan Academy for classes ranging from grade 4 to 12. The math classes taught without Khan Academy involved the teacher explaining the math concept to the students, demonstrating how to solve math problems related to the concept, and then assigning math workbook problems to the students to be solved individually or in groups. The classes with Khan Academy mainly involved the use of Khan Academy to practice math problems. The researchers documented the interactions between teachers and students when using Khan Academy and reported an increase in the active engagement of students and learning in math. Students reported they were motivated to attain mastery in math skills, and teachers reported that the students who struggled with math benefited from using Khan Academy. Although improvements were reported, the researchers did not collect objective data to support claims. Given observational studies infer causation (Sidman, [1952](#CR34)), it is possible other factors could have contributed to the reported behavior change.

Weeraratne and Chin ([2018](#CR44)) evaluated the impact of the video tutorials in Khan Academy in a blended learning environment for ninth-grade students in Sri Lanka. They compared the addition of Khan Academy’s video tutorials to weekly math lessons to regular math instruction on students’ performance using raw, standardized, and Item Response Theory adjusted scale test score using propensity score matching. They concluded that on average, Khan Academy resulted in increasing students' raw and scaled test scores by 3.77 and 3.15 percentage points, respectively, and standardized test scores by 0.20 standard deviations above the mean test score. This evaluation provided initial evidence that the use of Khan Academy could help improve student math performance. Although the results are promising, there are several gaps in knowing the effectiveness of Khan Academy in isolation. First, it is unclear how effective Khan Academy video tutorials would be in the absence of regular classroom instruction. In addition, Khan Academy’s practice component was not evaluated. Thus, it is unclear how effective Khan Academy is as a complete package in the absence or in addition to regular math instruction. Third, it is unclear the extent to which each individual exposed to Khan Academy video tutorials improved performance given data on individual participants were not reported. Regardless, these data may support the use of the video component in conjunction with regular math instruction.

One unpublished thesis that used objective measures and single-subject research methodology was Reed ([2019](#CR26)). Reed evaluated whether use of the video component of Khan Academy as a supplement to teacher-led instruction would increase the math quiz performance for six elementary school students with disabilities. During baseline, the researcher administered a 10-question quiz on the students’ targeted math skill. Next, the researcher presented the Khan Academy instructional video that corresponded to the targeted math skill immediately prior to administering the 10-question quiz. Khan Academy instructional videos increased quiz scores for two of the six participants; however, the increase was not to mastery (i.e., 90% correct across three consecutive quizzes). Given all participants did not reach mastery criteria, the researchers implemented behavioral skills training (BST). BST consisted of instructions (researcher explained how to complete the problem), modeling (demonstrated how to solve a problem using a white board and dry erase markers), rehearsal (presented a novel question for the participant to solve), and feedback (delivered praise or correct feedback based on problem completion, reviewed previous quiz) in isolation and combination with other modifications (i.e., increase in quiz time, reinforcement) to increase quiz scores. BST with and without additional modifications was required for all participants to meet mastery. Although these data suggest the instructional videos were ineffective in increasing quiz scores to mastery for elementary school students with disabilities when combined with teacher-led instruction, the teacher-led instruction and Khan Academy instructional videos did not necessarily align. Had the videos aligned with the teacher-led instruction or included more components of Khan Academy (e.g., practice problem sets), there may have been more significant increases in responding.

Given the limitations of previous research, it is important to objectively evaluate the effects of Khan Academy. Given the existing research did not evaluate Khan Academy as a complete package (e.g., Light & Pierson, [2014](#CR20); Reed, [2019](#CR26); Weeraratne & Chin, [2018](#CR44)), it is important to conduct studies that assess the effectiveness of Khan Academy as a whole. It would also be beneficial to understand the effectiveness of Khan Academy at an individual level, which may allow for greater insight into how students interact with Khan Academy to understand which components may be necessary for skill acquisition. Thus, the purpose of this study was to evaluate the effects of Khan Academy as a package intervention on targeted elementary math skills using objective measurements to assess changes in participant responding prior to and following Khan Academy.

## Method

### Participants and Setting

Elementary school students from suburban public schools were recruited as participants via email sent to personal and professional contacts. Six caregivers expressed interest to the researcher in their child participating in the study and completed a questionnaire to determine inclusion criteria. Criteria for participation included (1) access to a computer with a built-in camera, microphone, and internet service; (2) deficient score(s) in at least one math skill (e.g., compare two 3-digit numbers using > , = , and < ; fluently add and subtract within 100 using various strategies) falling at or below 60% correct despite previous instruction (60% was selected to reduce the ceiling effect associated with higher levels of responding); and (3) no use of additional math aids. Any caregivers or students not willing to stop the use of math aids for learning (e.g., math learning software such as Khan Academy, math workbooks, tutoring) other than the ones used in class during this study were excluded. Three participants were excluded from the study based on their high level of math performance.

The performance level in math was assessed using a two- to three-step process. First, the caregivers of the participant were required to submit the participant’s most recent report card issued by their school. The report cards submitted by caregivers listed each skill in math that was taught to the students and the participant’s progress within each skill across quarters (i.e., Quarter 1, Quarter 2, Quarter 3, Quarter 4). Participant progress was graded by the school as beginning (B; Student cannot yet complete the task independently and shows little understanding of the concept or skill), developing (D; Student shows some understanding. However, errors or misunderstandings still occur. Reminders, hints, and suggestions are needed to complete the task), or secure (S; Student demonstrates a firm grasp of the concepts/skills and can apply these concepts/skills correctly and independently). Following receipt of the report card, the researcher reviewed the report card and identified math skills in which the participant earned a proficiency level of “B” or “D.” Second, to verify there was a skill deficit, the researcher administered a preassessment based on common core standards to the participant in the math skill identified. If the participant scored less than 60% correct on the preassessment, that math skill was targeted for intervention. If the participant scored more than 60% correct on the preassessment, another math skill in which the student earned the proficiency level of “B” or “D” was selected, and a preassessment for that skill was administered. Third, if the participant scored more than 60% correct on all preassessments for skills graded as “B” or “D,” then a new math skill that had not yet been introduced to the participant was identified using the scope and sequence of the student’s school, and a preassessment was administered. Given difficulties in identifying skills for participants (i.e., five participants scored greater than 60% on all skills graded as “B” and “D”) and time constraints related to graduation requirements for the first author, we added this third step to the process.

Three elementary school students (Cindy, Aaron, and Ariana) participated in the study. All caregivers reported the students were neurotypical and received no academic accommodation from the school. Cindy was a white female in third grade at a public elementary school located in New Jersey. Of the students, 26.1% of students received free and reduced lunch. Their student population was composed of 3% Asian, 5% Hispanic, 7% Black, and 81% white. Cindy was not on free/reduced lunch. Her report card indicated a proficiency level of “D” in the skill of “Rounding whole numbers to the nearest 10 s and 100 s.” Cindy was administered a preassessment in rounding whole numbers to the nearest 10 s and 100 s. She scored 40% correct on the preassessment. Therefore, rounding to the nearest 10 s and 100 s was targeted for Cindy. Cindy’s teacher noted rounding was taught during the second quarter. Cindy started and completed the current study during the third quarter between February 20, 2022, and March 23, 2022. Therefore, there was no concurrent classroom instruction on rounding during the time of the study.

Aaron was an Asian American male in fourth grade at a public elementary school located in Illinois. Of the students, 15.5% of students received free and reduced lunch. Their student population was composed of 7% Hispanic, 9% Black, 34% white, and 45% Asian. Aaron was not on free/reduced lunch. He was in an accelerated math program in school. Aaron’s report card indicated a proficiency level of “B” in “Add and Subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions” and “Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction with unlike denominators using visual fraction models or equations.” He was administered a preassessment in both skills and scored 70% correct and 100% correct, respectively. Because no other skills were scored as “B” or “D,” he was administered a preassessment in “identify apparent relationship in two corresponding terms.” He scored a 0% correct on the preassessment. Therefore, identifying an apparent relationship in two corresponding terms was targeted for Aaron. Aaron’s teacher noted identifying an apparent relationship in two corresponding terms would be taught during the fourth quarter. Aaron started and completed the study during the third quarter between March 15, 2022, and March 20, 2022. Therefore, there was no concurrent instruction on identifying apparent relationship in two corresponding terms during the time of the study.

Ariana was an Asian American female in fourth grade. She attended the same school as Aaron and was Aaron’s twin sister. She was not on free/reduced lunch. Her report card indicated a proficiency level of “D” in “Fluently add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm” and “calculation area and perimeter.” She was administered a preassessment in both the skills and scored 100% for both the skills. Because no other skills were scored as “B” or “D,” she was administered a preassessment in “Adding hundredths and tenths.” She scored a 0% on the preassessment. Therefore, adding hundredths and tenths was targeted for Ariana. Ariana’s teacher noted adding hundredths and tenths would be taught during the fourth quarter. Ariana started and completed the study during the third quarter between March 15, 2022, and March 24, 2022. Therefore, there was no concurrent instruction on adding hundredths and tenths during the time of the study.

All sessions were conducted remotely via Zoom using a Health Insurance Portability and Accountability (HIPAA) compliant account. To access Zoom, the researcher sent the participant an email with the Zoom link and corresponding password. The participant completed sessions while seated in a chair at a table in a room with minimal distractions (e.g., limited items on table, few individuals in the room).

### Materials

The participants were required to have access to a computer with a built-in camera, microphone, and internet connectivity. Headphones were optional. Prior to the start of all sessions, the researcher provided the caregiver with a task analysis for accessing Zoom. The researcher created a Khan Academy account for each participant and provided the caregiver with a task analysis for accessing Khan Academy and their account on Khan Academy.

For targeted math skills, the researcher identified the corresponding Khan Academy skill and lesson that targeted the skill. A lesson in Khan Academy was composed of videos and sets of practice math problems related to the videos. The lesson for Cindy contained three videos and three sets of math problems. The lesson for Aaron contained three videos and two sets of math problems. The lesson for Ariana contained two videos and two sets of math problems.

Ten worksheets and their corresponding solution sheets, each containing 10 problems in the skill identified for each participant, were created. The worksheets and solution sheets were auto generated using a math worksheet generator for Common Core standards ([www.commoncoresheets.com](http://www.commoncoresheets.com); see supplemental materials for an example). All worksheets were converted to fillable PDF documents. These worksheets were used for the preassessment and quizzes during baseline and post-Khan Academy. No worksheets or math problems were repeated for a participant.

### Response Measurement and Interobserver Agreement (IOA)

Three trained data collectors collected data during this study. All data collectors were enrolled in a master’s program for applied behavior analysis and certified as Registered Behavior Technicians. The data collectors recorded data from completed worksheets following the preassessment, baseline, and post-Khan Academy. The primary dependent variables were the number of correct and incorrect math problems. A correct math problem was scored when the answers recorded by the participant matched the answers recorded on the solution sheet provided to the observer. An incorrect math problem was scored when the answers did not match. Percentage correct was calculated by dividing the number of correct math problems by the total number of math problems and multiplying by 100.

To better understand how participants were performing during Khan Academy and the types and amount of hints they accessed during Khan Academy, data collectors recorded descriptive data on the duration of video hints watched, the frequency of step-by-step textual hints accessed, and the number of correct problems while completing autogenerated practice problems on Khan Academy. To score the duration of video hints watched, data collectors started a timer when the participant started the video hint and ended the timer when the participant stopped the video. This measure was converted to a percentage by dividing the number of minutes a participant watched a video by the length of the video and multiplying by 100. The frequency of hints accessed was recorded on a problem-by-problem basis and was scored when the participant selected “Get a hint” or “Get another hint.” This measure was converted to hints per problem measure by dividing the number of hints accessed by the number of practice problems within the problem set. We scored by question rather than by practice set as each practice set varied in the number of questions (range: 4–7 questions). A correct math problem was scored when Khan Academy indicated independent completion of the problem (i.e., positive message such as “Good work” or “Great work” and open circle corresponding to the problem changed to solid green). The number of correct problems was converted to a percentage by dividing the number of correct problems by the total number of practice problems within the problem set and multiplying by 100.

A second, independent observer scored the number of correct and incorrect math problems during an average of 37.9% (range: 33.3%–42.9%) of sessions across participants during baseline and post-Khan Academy sessions and scored duration of videos, frequency of hints accessed, and number of correct problems during 55.5% (range: 33.3%–100%) of Khan Academy sessions. To calculate IOA for correct and incorrect math problems and number of correct problems while practicing problems on Khan Academy, the number of agreements between observers were identified. An agreement was scored when both observers recorded the same answer as correct or incorrect, whereas a disagreement was scored when observers recorded the same answer as correct and incorrect. IOA was calculated by dividing the number of agreements by the total number of agreements and disagreements, multiplying by 100. IOA for the duration of videos watched was calculated by first aggregating all timings into one summed duration for each observer and then dividing the smaller duration by the larger duration, multiplying by 100. To calculate the IOA for frequency of textual hints accessed, the total number of problems in which both the observers agreed on whether hints were accessed was divided by the total number of problems and multiplied by 100. Across participants, mean agreement was 100% for correct and incorrect math problems, duration of videos, and number of correct problems across participants. It should be noted that no participants watched videos during Khan Academy while practicing problems. Therefore, the summed durations were always 0 s, resulting in 100% agreement for this measure across participants. Mean agreement was 94.43% (range: 83.3%–100%) for hints accessed across participants.

### Treatment Integrity

Treatment integrity was assessed during an average of 39.2% (range: 33.3%–40%) of sessions across participants in each phase of the study to identify the extent to which the researcher implemented study procedures as written including presentation of worksheets, relevant instructions, 2-min warning, Khan Academy videos, prompts to stay on-task, and absence of feedback or reinforcers. A second observer recorded the researcher’s adherence to the intervention plan by marking each checklist item with a “Yes” if the researcher adhered to the intervention plan or “No” if the researcher failed to adhere to the intervention plan. The percentage of steps implemented correctly were calculated by dividing the total number of “Yes” by total number of steps and multiplying 100. Mean treatment integrity was 100% across all participants.

### Procedure

#### Prestudy Survey

Prior to the start of sessions, the participant completed a prestudy survey on their feelings towards math, their eagerness to improve at math, and their comfort in learning math online before they were introduced to Khan Academy. This survey consisted of five questions. The participant rated their responses using a 5-point graphic Likert scale which ranged from awful to fantastic. A rating of 1 corresponded to awful, and a rating of 5 corresponded to fantastic.

#### General Procedures

Sessions were conducted based on participant availability. On average, sessions were conducted 1.3 days per week (range: 1–2), two times per day (range: 1–4). Prior to the first session, the researcher provided the caregiver with a task analysis for accessing Zoom. At the beginning of each session, the researcher requested the participant to share their screen using the “share screen” function of Zoom. If needed, the researcher provided additional verbal directions on how to use the screen sharing function, open worksheets, and access the math lesson on Khan Academy. If the researcher was unable to help the participant (e.g., opening the worksheet or sharing their screen on Zoom), then the researcher requested the caregiver to help the participant. The researcher typically requested help from the caregiver during the first session of baseline and Khan Academy for each participant. Following all sessions, the researcher thanked the participants for their time. If multiple sessions were conducted in a day, the participants were offered the choice of a brief break (i.e., 5–10 min) or conducting another session at a later time in the day.

##### **Baseline**

During baseline sessions, the researcher greeted the participant and provided the participant with a worksheet containing 10 math problems in the targeted math skill via email or through the chat function in Zoom, depending on the preference of the caregiver. The researcher gave the instruction,

> Today you will be completing the worksheet. Please complete the worksheet the best you can. You have 15 min to complete the worksheet. You can use a blank sheet of paper for calculations. If you do use one, please hold it up for me at the end of the session. I will not be able to answer any questions when you are working on your worksheet. If you are done before 15 min, please do let me know and we can end the session. Are you ready? Your timer starts now.

If the participant was off-task or looked away from the worksheet for more than 10 s, the researcher instructed the participant to stay focused on their work. If the participant asked questions, the researcher responded with “I cannot answer any questions right now.” When 2 min remained, the researcher gave a 2-min warning (i.e., “You have 2 min remaining.”). No other prompts, feedback, or reinforcement were provided during the session. When 15 min elapsed or the participant indicated they finished the worksheet, the researcher requested the participant to display their work completed on the blank sheet. The first baseline session served as the pre-assessment and confirmed the participant lacked proficiency (i.e., scored 60% correct or less) in the skill being targeted. The participant’s subsequent performance during baseline confirmed there was little to no change in the performance level prior to introducing Khan Academy.

##### **Khan Academy**

During Khan Academy sessions, the researcher greeted the participant and gave the instruction,

> We will begin with watching videos and then practice the corresponding problem sets. You can use a blank sheet of paper for any calculations. If you have difficulty solving a math problem, you can either access hints by watching videos or by accessing step-by-step textual hints.

The participant watched Khan Academy’s instructional videos corresponding to the targeted math skill for approximately 5 to 10 min (depending on the length of the video). Once the participants watched the video(s) in full, they completed autogenerated practice problems embedded within Khan Academy.

Each set of practice problems contained four to seven practice problems that varied on each attempt. Within the sets of practice problems, the participant could access video hints or step-by-step textual hints when unsure how to solve a problem or following an error. The textual hints were revealed in an incremental manner such that each click on “Get another hint” revealed only one step at a time. If an error was made, a prompt “Not Quite. Get help or move on.” was provided. If the participant selected get help, they were provided with corresponding videos and textual hints. If the participant selected to move on, the participant was presented with the next problem. The circle that corresponded to the question was filled with solid grey. If the participant independently solved the problem correctly in the absence of additional videos or hints, praise (e.g., “Nice work!” “Great job”) with visual (i.e., bright confetti, golden star) and auditory stimuli (i.e., ding) were provided. In addition, the circle that corresponded to the question was filled in with solid green.

The participant was allowed to use a blank sheet of paper and writing utensils to do calculations if they needed. If the participant was off-task or looked away from the computer screen for more than 10 s, the researcher prompted “Please stay focused on your work.” After practicing math problems for 10–15 min, the researcher asked the participant to display their calculations if they used a blank sheet of paper.

Khan Academy assigned proficiency based on the participant’s responding during practice math problems. At the beginning of the lesson, the skill was assigned “No Level.” If the participant scored less than 70% correct on all sets of practice problems, the skill was assigned “Attempted.” If the participant scored greater than 70% correct but less than 100%, the skill was assigned “Familiar.” Finally, if the participant scored 100% correct, the skill was assigned “Proficient.” If the participant was proficient in the skill as identified by Khan Academy, they moved to post-Khan Academy. If the participant was not proficient in the skill following one exposure to the instructional videos and each practice problem, they completed a Khan Academy booster session.

##### **Khan Academy Booster**

The researcher conducted a booster session when the participant did not reach proficiency in the targeted math skill. Booster sessions were similar to Khan Academy; however, the participant was given the choice to rewatch the instructional videos (both participants selected to forgo the instructional videos). Similar to Khan Academy, participants completed practice problems. Participants were required to complete the practice problems to proficiency.

##### **Post-Khan Academy**

Post-Khan Academy sessions were conducted once the participant attained proficiency as indicated by Khan Academy. The post-Khan Academy sessions were conducted similar to the baseline. Mastery criteria were three consecutive worksheets at 90% correct.

#### Experimental Design

We used a nonconcurrent multiple baseline design across participants (Harvey et al., [2004](#CR10)) to evaluate the effects of our independent variable on our dependent variable. A nonconcurrent multiple baseline design allowed for flexibility in scheduling and conducting sessions. First, a pre-assessment was conducted to verify the participant lacked proficiency in the targeted math skill. Second, baseline was conducted until a steady state was observed. Third, we staggered the implementation of Khan Academy across participants such that changes in responding across participants could be assessed at different points in time.

#### Social Validity

At the conclusion of the study, the caregivers and the participants completed a poststudy survey. The participant poststudy survey was administered to understand whether the participant’s feelings towards math, their eagerness to improve at math, and their comfort in learning math online changed following exposure to Khan Academy. The survey consisted of six questions similar to the prestudy survey in which the participant rated their responses using a 5-point graphic Likert scale which ranged from awful to fantastic where a 1 represented awful and 5 represented fantastic; however, the poststudy survey contained two additional questions related to Khan Academy that were not relevant prior to the start of the study. The caregiver poststudy survey was administered to understand the acceptability of Khan Academy from the caregiver’s perspective. The survey consisted of five questions. Caregivers rated their agreement with survey items using a 3-point Likert scale ranging from “disagree” to “completely agree.”

([2018](#CR9)). Sessions are scaled to the x-axis, percentage is scaled to the left y-axis, and rate is scaled to the right y-axis. Closed data points depict the percentage correct on math worksheets during baseline and post-Khan Academy, closed bars depict the percentage correct on practice problems during Khan Academy, open squares depict the percentage of video hints watched (i.e., during practice problems during Khan Academy), and open circles depict the rate of textual hints (i.e., number of textual hints accessed per practice problem) accessed during practice problems during Khan Academy. Gaps in sessions denote where there was at least 1 day between sessions.

## Discussion

The purpose of the present study was to evaluate the effectiveness of Khan Academy in teaching math to elementary school students using pre- and post-worksheet assessments. In addition, we collected descriptive data on participant performance during Khan Academy lessons and the hints that were accessed during Khan Academy problem sets. All three participants acquired and mastered the targeted math skill following exposure to one (Ariana) or three (Aaron and Cindy) Khan Academy sessions. Most peer-reviewed, published research has evaluated the effectiveness of Khan Academy for math at the classroom level, used descriptive methods, and lacked objective measures at an individual level (e.g., Cargile & Harkness, [2015](#CR2); Light & Pierson, [2014](#CR20); Weeraratne & Chin, [2018](#CR44)). In addition, previous research has evaluated single components of Khan Academy rather than Khan Academy as a whole (e.g., Light & Pierson, [2014](#CR20); Weeraratne & Chin, [2018](#CR44)). Overall, Khan Academy was effective in teaching a targeted math skill that had been previously presented at school for one participant (Cindy) and a novel targeted math skill for two participants (Aaron and Ariana). args.summary:
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in Behavior Analysis in Practice (2024) by Poonam A. Patil and Jessica F. Juanico from the University of Kansas, evaluating the effectiveness of Khan Academy in teaching elementary math skills using objective, single-subject methodology.

**Background:** The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the need for systematic evaluation of online educational tools. Khan Academy is a popular free platform with 120+ million users in 190+ countries. Previous research on Khan Academy has largely used descriptive methods (interviews, observations), group designs, or evaluated single components rather than the complete package. Little research has used objective measures at the individual level.

**Methodology:** Three neurotypical elementary students participated (Cindy, 3rd grade; Aaron and Ariana, 4th grade) via remote Zoom sessions. A nonconcurrent multiple baseline design across participants was used. Participants completed pre-worksheet assessments (baseline), then used Khan Academy (videos + practice problems), then completed post-Khan Academy worksheets. Mastery criteria was 90% correct across three consecutive worksheets. Targeted skills included: rounding to nearest 10s/100s (Cindy), identifying relationships in corresponding terms (Aaron), and adding hundredths/tenths (Ariana).

**Results:** All three participants acquired and mastered targeted math skills following Khan Academy exposure. Cindy (rounded to nearest 10s/100s) scored 40% in baseline, reached 90% mastery after two Khan Academy sessions plus a booster. Aaron (identifying relationships) scored 0% in baseline, reached 90-100% after two Khan Academy sessions plus a booster. Ariana (adding hundredths/tenths) scored 0% in baseline, reached 90-100% after just one Khan Academy session. Interobserver agreement averaged 100% for correct/incorrect problems and 94.43% for hints accessed. Treatment integrity was 100%.

**Participant Engagement with Khan Academy:** During Khan Academy sessions, no participants watched video hints during practice problems. Use of textual hints was minimal (0-0.71 hints per problem). Social validity surveys showed high acceptability from both participants and caregivers.

**Conclusions:** Khan Academy was effective as a complete package intervention for teaching elementary math skills. The study addresses gaps in previous research by using objective measurements, single-subject design, and evaluating Khan Academy as a whole rather than individual components. The authors note Khan Academy's components align with behavior analytic principles (BST: instructions, modeling, rehearsal, feedback) and Keller's Personalized System of Instruction.

[Skip to content](#content "Skip to content")



# Multiple Studies Show Khan Academy Drives Learning Gains: Evidence for Our Platform’s Effectiveness

*By [Phil Grimaldi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/phillip-grimaldi/), Senior Efficacy and Research Scientist at Khan Academy.*

The evidence is clear—Khan Academy works. Study after study confirms that using Khan Academy leads to better math performance and attitudes. Whether it’s higher standardized test scores, better grades, or increased college readiness, the data tells a consistent story. Khan Academy’s personalized and engaging platform helps students worldwide achieve more in math. In this key post, we share a selection of high-quality research studies that have evaluated the effectiveness of Khan Academy. The studies are organized by the quality of evidence, according to the [Every Child Succeeds Act (ESSA)](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs/regions/midwest/pdf/blogs/RELMW-ESSA-Tiers-Video-Handout-508.pdf)*.* Read about how our platform outpaces typical growth rates and drives learning outcomes.

### Well-designed and implemented experimental studies (Tier 1, Strong evidence)

Students in schools with Khan Academy and lab-in-charge who ensured high level of usage (~1h per week) scored 0.44 to 0.47 standard deviations higher than students in the control group (Khan Academy only without lab-in-charge) on the end-of-year mathematics assessment, according to Oreopoulos, Keyes-Krisakowski and Agrawal (2026), who conducted a randomized-control trial of ~5500 students across 74 schools in India. [[pdf](https://www.nber.org/papers/w34683)]

Students who used Khan Academy as part of a year-long mastery learning intervention improved their end-of-year math scores by .12 to .22 standard deviations, according to Oreopoulos, Gibbs, Jenson, & Price (2024), who conducted a randomized-control trial of nearly 11,000 students in grades 3-8. [[pdf](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w32388/w32388.pdf)]

Weekly usage of Khan Academy resulted in positive effects on math scores and attitudes towards math when implemented with adequate support, according to Ferman, Finamor, & Lima (2019), who conducted a large-scale randomized-control trial across 157  primary schools in Brazil. [[pdf](https://mpra.ub.uni-muenchen.de/94736/1/MPRA_paper_94736.pdf)]

Supplemental use of Khan Academy resulted in better math scores than teacher-only interventions, according to Buchel, Jakob,  Kuhnhanss,  Seffen, &  Brunetti (2019), who conducted a large-scale randomized-control trial with ~3500 third- through sixth-grade students in El Salvador. [[pdf](https://www.consciente.ch/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/CALImpact_Evaluation_Report_April19.pdf)]

Students who used Khan Academy during a 19-day summer program had better algebra-readiness scores, according to Snipes, Huang, Jaquet, & Finkelstein (2015), who conducted a randomized-control trial with 496 seventh-grade students in a Silicon Valley school district.  [[pdf](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs/regions/west/pdf/REL_2015096.pdf)]

### Well-designed and implemented quasi-experimental studies (Tier 2, Moderate evidence)

Students who increased their usage of Khan Academy by 30m per week or 60 skills per year saw increases in test score gains between .09SD and .18SD on MAP Growth assessment. [A study published in the *Proceedings of National Academy of Sciences*](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2507708123) – a top peer-reviewed journal – used a rigorous methodology to account for both teacher and student characteristics in a longitudinal dataset of around 200K students across hundreds of districts (Eames, T, Brunskill, E, Yamkovenko, B., Weatherhold, K, and Oreopoulos, P (2026)). [[pdf](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2507708123)]

Students who increased their usage of Khan Academy over three school years saw gains on end of year state achievement test (NJSLA). A three year-panel study, with teacher, student, and year fixed effects in Newark, NJ found that increasing Khan Academy by 18 hours or 60 skills mastered year over year can almost double the average year to year NJSLA gains. (Yamkovenko, B., Grimaldi, P, (2025)). [[pdf](https://blog.khanacademy.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/Newark_White_Paper-2.pdf)]

Students who increased their usage of Khan Academy from year to year saw corresponding gains in learning as measured by MAP growth scores. A quasi-experimental study with student and teacher fixed effects to account for student ability and teacher quality found that increasing usage by 30-60 skills year to year can lead to 15-30pp gains in learning. (Weatherholtz, K., Grimaldi, P., Yamkovenko, B., Hill, K.M. (2024)). [[pdf](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-72315-5_32)]

Students who used supplemental Khan Academy in blended classrooms also had higher performance on a standardized math assessment,  according to a quasi-experimental study with ninth-grade students in Sri Lanka (Weeraratne & Chin, 2018). [[pdf](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1201489.pdf)]

Students who used Khan Academy were more likely to have better math performance than a traditional math intervention program, according to the results of a quasi-experimental study of third- and sixth-grade students in Guatemala (Manuas, 2016). [[pdf](https://learningequality.org/media/FUNSEPA_Final_Evaluation_Report_27May2016.pdf)]

### Well-designed and implemented correlational studies (Tier 3, Promising evidence)

Students who used Khan Academy MAP Accelerator for 30 minutes or more per week saw better MAP Growth math scores compared to students who used MAP Accelerator for less time. This was the main finding of a correlational study with statistical controls conducted by Weatherholtz, Grimaldi, & Hill (2022).  [[pdf](http://khan.co/MATechReport2022)]

Students who spent more time using Khan Academy’s Official SAT prep tool were more likely to score higher on the SAT, according to correlational studies with controls (Weatherholtz, Grimaldi, Hicks, & Hill, 2020; College Board, 2017). [[pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1RCzUeOGhINzZ2OhEr-yciF1VmU_B_vNg/view?usp=sharing)][[pdf](https://drive.google.com/file/d/19khVKUexqi57vrLIAi8qGs7tCwqojy8J/view)]

Use of Khan Academy among middle school students in the Long Beach Unified School District was linked to better performance on a standardized assessment, according to a correlational study by Hill, Weatherholtz, & Chattergoon (2018). [[pdf](https://cdn.kastatic.org/downloads/2018_LBUSD_Efficacy_Study_Research_Brief.pdf)]

Community college students who used Khan Academy were more likely to score higher on the ACCUPLACER math assessment, according to a study by Chan, O’Conner, & Peat (2016). [[pdf](http://www.nebhe.org/info/pdf/policy/Results_and_Lessons_from_DMDP_Sept_2016.pdf)]
