### 2.3 Study selection protocol

Following initial duplicate removal in Covidence systematic review software (n = 250 excluded from 3,500 records), two independent reviewers conducted blinded screening. Title/abstract assessment prioritized relevance to the four predefined cognitive domains, followed by full-text evaluation against inclusion criteria. Inter-rater reliability during title/abstract screening demonstrated substantial agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.78). Discrepancies were resolved through Covidence's structured workflow:

1.   1.
Automated Flagging:System-generated alerts identified conflicting decisions

2.   2.
Blinded Reassessment:Reviewers independently reevaluated flagged records before consensus discussion

3.   3.
Third-Reviewer Arbitration:Unresolved conflicts underwent adjudication by a psychology subject-matter expert

4.   4.
Documentation:All resolution rationales were logged within Covidence to maintain an auditable decision trail

This multi-stage verification process minimized selection bias and enhanced methodological reproducibility. Fifteen studies ultimately satisfied all inclusion requirements (see Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#Fig1): PRISMA Flow Diagram in Appendix A).

### 2.4 Quality assessment & synthesis approach

**Methodological Rigor**: Study quality was appraised using design-specific tools:

*   **RCTs:**Cochrane RoB 2 evaluated selection, performance, detection, attrition, and reporting bias (categorized as low/some concerns/high risk)

*   **Observational studies:**Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) scored selection (0–4), comparability (0–2), and outcome ascertainment (0–3); higher totals (max 9) indicated lower bias

*   **Qualitative studies:**CASP Qualitative Checklist assessed 10 domains (e.g., aims, methodology, ethics) via yes/no/can’t tell ratings

Studies failing empirical quality thresholds (RoB 2 "high risk", NOS < 5, CASP < 7/10) were excluded per systematic review best practices:

*   NOS < 5 reflects significant limitations in observational design alignment with Cochrane standards [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR5 " Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, version 6.3 (2022). Cochrane, 2022. 
                  https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/archive/v6.3
                  
                . Accessed on March 2 2025.")]

*   CASP < 7 indicates inadequate methodological transparency per CASP guidelines [[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR6 "Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP). CASP Qualitative Checklist. 2018. (Online ) Available at: https://casp-uk.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/CASP-Qualitative-Checklist-2018.pdf. Accessed on March 4 2025. 
                  https://casp-uk.net/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/CASP-Qualitative-Checklist-2018.pdf
                  
                ")]

### 3.2 Narrative synthesis

#### 3.2.1 Attention

Multiple studies reported that digital multitasking particularly via smartphones and social media fragments attention and reduces sustained focus [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR7 "Feng J, Bian Y.                   https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2020.106510
                  
                ."), [8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR8 "Uncapher MR, Lin L, Rosen LD, Kirkorian HL, Baron NS, Bailey K, et al. Media multitasking and cognitive, psychological, neural, and learning differences. Pediatrics. 2017;140(Supplement 2):S62–6. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2016-1758D
                  
                .")]. Adolescents were especially vulnerable to attention decline due to frequent task-switching and notification overload [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR9 "Shanmugasundaram K, Lee J, Smith T.                 .")]. However, action video games were found to enhance perceptual accuracy and task-switching speed, suggesting potential cognitive benefits when digital tools are used strategically [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR10 "Bediou B, Adams DM, Mayer RE, Tipton E, Green CS, Bavelier D. Meta-analysis of action video game impact on perceptual, attentional, and cognitive skills. Psychol Bull. 2018;144(1):77–110.

#### 3.2.2 Memory

The reviewed studies revealed a dual impact on memory. On one hand, educational apps supported metacognitive awareness and self-regulated learning [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR11 "Greene JA, Copeland DZ, Yu SB. Digital tools and metacognitive awareness in learning: a longitudinal study. Educ Psychol Rev. 2019;31(4):987–1012. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09485-1
                  
                .")]. On the other hand, over-reliance on digital tools for information storage, such as search engines was associated with reduced intrinsic memory and impaired autobiographical recall [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR12 "Hamilton RJ, Wadhwa K, Joinson AN. Digital technology and cognitive overload in educational settings: a qualitative exploration. J Educ Technol. 2023;45(2):234–50."), [13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR13 "Tamir DI, Templeton EM, Ward AF, Zaki J. Media usage diminishes memory for personal experiences. J Exp Psychol Gen. 2018;147(10):1471–87. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000469
                  
                .")].

#### 3.2.3 Decision-making

Access to real-time digital information was shown to improve analytical decision-making in some contexts [[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR14 "Roussos P. Multitasking and cognitive performance across demographics: a meta-analysis. Cogn Sci. 2023;47(3):e13245. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/cogs.13245
                  
                .")]. However, data saturation and algorithm-driven environments often led users to rely on heuristics, undermining critical thinking and deep analysis.

#### 3.2.4 Neuroplasticity

Several studies demonstrated that digital technologies can enhance neuroplasticity, particularly through structured interventions like video game training [[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR15 "Anguera JA, Boccanfuso J, Rintoul JL, Al-Hashimi O, Faraji F, Janowich J, et al. Video game training enhances cognitive control in older adults. Nature. 2020;501(7465):97–101. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12486
                  
                .")]. These tools improved spatial reasoning and cognitive flexibility, especially in older adults. Conversely, excessive or addictive digital use was linked to structural brain changes, including diminished impulse control [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR16 "Kühn S, Gallinat J. Smartphone addiction and its impact on attention, memory, and executive functions. Addict Biol. 2019;24(4):712–22. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/adb.12610
                  
                .")].

#### 3.2.5 Cross-cutting themes

*   In low-resource settings, interactive digital tools improved problem-solving and learning outcomes [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR17 "Oduaran C, Okorie N. Digital media and cognitive development in African children: a cross-sectional study. Child Dev Perspect. 2021;15(2):89–97.")].

*   The digital divide exacerbated cognitive inequalities, particularly in underserved communities [[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR18 "Nkomo LM, Ndlovu N. Digital divide and cognitive inequalities in South African communities. J Soc Inclus. 2023;14(1):112–30.")].

*   The cognitive impact of digital technologies varied significantly by age, context, and design quality.

## 4 Discussions

The results of this review underscore the dual nature of digital technologies’ cognitive impacts, aligning with Cognitive Load Theory, Multimedia Learning Theory, the Document Literacy Framework, and Neuroplasticity Models. These frameworks used to explain how digital technologies can either impair or enhance cognitive domains, depending on.their design, context, and usage patterns.

### 4.1 Cognitive load and overload: explicit linkages

Cognitive Load Theory posits that the brain’s finite working memory becomes strained when overwhelmed by extraneous stimuli. Multimedia Learning Theory extends this by emphasizing that poorly designed digital technologies (e.g., cluttered educational apps) exacerbate extraneous load, while optimized designs (e.g., integrated text and visuals) enhance learning by supporting dual-channel processing. This review’s results validate these frameworks through through three key mechanisms:

Attention Fragmentation: Media multitasking aligns with Cognitive Load Theory’s concept of extraneous load and the Document Literacy Framework’s emphasis on navigational challenges, as switching between digital tasks or hyperlinks depletes working memory, leading to shallow processing. Digital Technologies multitasking (e.g., switching between social media and work tasks) directly aligns with the theory’s concept of cognitive load, as divided attention depletes working memory resources, leading to shallow processing and reduced retention [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR7 "Feng J, Bian Y. Social media usage and cognitive processes: a meta-analytic review. Comput Human Behav. 2020;113:106510. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2020.106510
                  
                ."), [8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR8 "Uncapher MR, Lin L, Rosen LD, Kirkorian HL, Baron NS, Bailey K, et al. Media multitasking and cognitive, psychological, neural, and learning differences. Pediatrics. 2017;140(Supplement 2):S62–6. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2016-1758D
                  
                .")].

Cognitive Overload: Excessive screen time in educational settings [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR12 "Hamilton RJ, Wadhwa K, Joinson AN. Digital technology and cognitive overload in educational settings: a qualitative exploration. J Educ Technol. 2023;45(2):234–50.")] mirrors the theory’s warning about cognitive load, where non-essential stimuli (e.g., notifications) compete for mental bandwidth, impairing deep engagement with learning materials.

Heuristic Reliance: Data-saturated environments push users toward superficial decision-making [[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR14 "Roussos P. Multitasking and cognitive performance across demographics: a meta-analysis. Cogn Sci. 2023;47(3):e13245. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/cogs.13245
                  
                .")], reflecting how cognitive overload triggers germane load depletion, forcing reliance on mental shortcuts particularly when evaluating multiple digital technologies.

### 4.2 Multimedia learning and design optimization

Multimedia Learning Theory emphasizes the importance of aligning digital content with cognitive principles. Studies reviewed here showed that well-designed educational apps those that integrate text, visuals, and audio effectively can reduce extraneous cognitive load and promote deeper learning [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR11 "Greene JA, Copeland DZ, Yu SB. Digital tools and metacognitive awareness in learning: a longitudinal study. Educ Psychol Rev. 2019;31(4):987–1012. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09485-1
                  
                .")]. This highlights the value of coherence and signaling principles in digital learning environments.

### 4.3 Document literacy and navigational demands

The Document Literacy Framework explains how navigating complex digital texts (e.g., hyperlinked documents) requires strategic reading and evaluation skills. Poor navigation was linked to increased cognitive load and reduced comprehension, particularly among younger users. Conversely, tools that support document literacy, such as clear layouts and guided prompts enhanced memory and decision-making.

### 4.4 Neuroplasticity models: strengthening adaptability

Neuroplasticity Models highlight the brain’s ability to rewire neural pathways. Multimedia Learning Theory and the Document Literacy Framework complement this by showing how digital technologies foster adaptive learning:

Positive Neuroplasticity: Action video games enhance perceptual accuracy and task-switching efficiency [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR10 "Bediou B, Adams DM, Mayer RE, Tipton E, Green CS, Bavelier D. Meta-analysis of action video game impact on perceptual, attentional, and cognitive skills. Psychol Bull. 2018;144(1):77–110. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000130
                  
                .")], illustrating _experience-dependent plasticity_ where repeated skill-based interactions strengthen neural circuits associated with visual processing. Similarly, educational apps promoting metacognitive awareness [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR11 "Greene JA, Copeland DZ, Yu SB. Digital tools and metacognitive awareness in learning: a longitudinal study. Educ Psychol Rev. 2019;31(4):987–1012. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09485-1
                  
                .")] leverage multimedia design to support self-directed plasticity, as reflective practices rewire prefrontal networks governing self-regulation.

Negative Neuroplasticity: Conversely, addictive smartphone usage correlates with structural changes in impulse-control regions [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR11 "Greene JA, Copeland DZ, Yu SB. Digital tools and metacognitive awareness in learning: a longitudinal study. Educ Psychol Rev. 2019;31(4):987–1012. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09485-1
                  
                .")], exacerbated by challenges in navigating complex digital texts and underscoring maladaptive plasticity where habitual overuse reinforces neural pathways linked to compulsive behaviors, diminishing executive function.

Aging and Neuroplasticity: Video game training enhances cognitive control in older adults [[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR15 "Anguera JA, Boccanfuso J, Rintoul JL, Al-Hashimi O, Faraji F, Janowich J, et al. Video game training enhances cognitive control in older adults. Nature. 2020;501(7465):97–101. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12486
                  
                .")], supported by multimedia designs that reduce cognitive load and document literacy skills that improve information integration, challenging the notion of rigid brain aging and showcasing technology’s potential to sustain cognitive flexibility.

### 4.5 Integrative perspective

The interplay among Cognitive Load Theory, Multimedia Learning Theory, the Document Literacy Framework, and Neuroplasticity Models resolves the paradox: digital technologies can overload cognition when they exceed cognitive capacities or require complex navigation, but they enhance cognitive processes when designed and used strategically to align with human cognitive and neural potential. This integrated framework informs practical strategies for optimizing the cognitive impacts of digital technologies across attention, memory, decision-making, and neuroplasticity, as outlined below:

Strategic Design: Educational technologies should minimize extraneous cognitive load through distraction-free interfaces, as advocated by Cognitive Load Theory, while incorporating Multimedia Learning Theory’s principles, such as coherence (e.g., avoiding irrelevant visuals) and signaling (e.g., highlighting key information), to enhance learning efficiency. For example, apps with metacognitive prompts re duce cognitive overload while fostering self-regulated learning [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR11 "Greene JA, Copeland DZ, Yu SB. Digital tools and metacognitive awareness in learning: a longitudinal study. Educ Psychol Rev. 2019;31(4):987–1012. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09485-1
                  
                .")]. Similarly, the Document Literacy Framework suggests designing digital interfaces with clear navigational cues to support efficient processing of electronic texts, reducing atten tion fragmentation. These designs leverage neuroplasticity by promoting focused engagement that strengthens neural pathways associated with cognitive skills [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR19 "Doidge N. The brain that changes itself: stories of personal triumph from the frontiers of brain science. New York: Viking Press, 2007.")].

Contextual Outcomes: The cognitive impact of digital technologies varies by dose, design, and developmental stage. For instance, action video games improve spatial reasoning in older adults [[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR15 "Anguera JA, Boccanfuso J, Rintoul JL, Al-Hashimi O, Faraji F, Janowich J, et al. Video game training enhances cognitive control in older adults. Nature. 2020;501(7465):97–101. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12486
                  
                .")] by leveraging neuroplasticity [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR19 "Doidge N. The brain that changes itself: stories of personal triumph from the frontiers of brain science. New York: Viking Press, 2007.")]. However, excessive use in adolescents risks cognitive overload [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR9 "Shanmugasundaram K, Lee J, Smith T. Excessive smartphone use and reduced attention span in adolescents: a longitudinal study. J Adolesc. 2023;94:102–15. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.adolescence.2023.02.007
                  
                .")], as predicted by Cognitive Load Theory. Multimedia Learning Theory explains how well designed games with balanced visual and auditory elements enhance attention and memory, while the Document Literacy Framework highlights that poorly structured digital texts (e.g., complex hypertexts) can exacerbate attention fragmentation in younger users. Tailoring digital technologies to developmental needs ensures cognitive empowerment over overload.

Skill Development: Digital literacy programs should teach skills for navigating and evaluating digital technologies, particularly electronic texts, as emphasized by the Document Literacy Framework. Training users to strategically process web based content (e.g., evaluating source credibility, integrating multiple documents) enhances attention, memory, and decision-making. Multimedia Learning Theory supports incorporating interactive tutorials that use dual-channel processing to teach these skills effectively. Such training fosters neuroplasticity growth Pascual-Leone et al. [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR2 "Pascual-Leone A, Amedi A, Fregni F, Merabet LB. The plastic human brain cortex. Annu Rev Neurosci. 2005;28(1):377–401. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.neuro.27.070203.144216
                  
                .")], by encouraging adaptive cognitive strategies while mitigating cognitive overload from information-rich digital environments [[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR20 "Sweller J. Cognitive load during problem solving: effects on learning. Cogn Sci. 1988;12(2):257–85. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog1202_4
                  
                .")]. These insights call for policies that prioritize digital literacy, equipping users to navigate digital technologies in ways that respect cognitive limits while harnessing their potential for growth. Educators should adopt distraction-minimized, multimedia-optimized tools and teach document literacy skills to support effective learning. Policymakers should promote equitable access to such technologies and training, particularly in low-resource settings, to ensure cognitive benefits are universally accessible.

### 4.6 Limitations

This review advances understanding of digital technologies' dual cognitive impacts by integrating Cognitive Load Theory [[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR20 "Sweller J. Cognitive load during problem solving: effects on learning. Cogn Sci. 1988;12(2):257–85. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog1202_4
                  
                .")], Multimedia Learning Theory [[21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR21 "Mayer RE. Multimedia learning. In: Ross BH, editor. Psychology of learning and motivation. San Diego, CA: Academic Press; 2002. p. 85–139.")], Neuroplasticity Models Pascual-Leone et al. [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR2 "Pascual-Leone A, Amedi A, Fregni F, Merabet LB. The plastic human brain cortex. Annu Rev Neurosci. 2005;28(1):377–401. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.neuro.27.070203.144216
                  
                .")], and the Document Literacy Framework [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR22 "Route JF. The skills of document use: from text comprehension to web-based learning. London, New York: Routledge, 2006.")], offering practical strategies for balanced digital engagement. However, several limitations merit consideration.

First, the restriction to English-language studies may have excluded relevant non-English research, introducing language bias. Second, the exclusion of grey literature (e.g., technical reports, dissertations, conference proceedings, and industry or government publications) risks publication bias, potentially overemphasizing positive or statistically significant outcomes. Grey literature often includes unpublished null findings, real-world applications, or data from underrepresented regions, such as industry reports on workplace digital technology usage or government surveys on digital technology access in rural communities, which might offer contrasting insights to peer-reviewed studies. For instance, industry-driven evaluations of educational apps could reveal practical challenges in implementation not highlighted in academic trials, while theses might explore longitudinal effects of digital technologies in specific populations.

Geographically, while studies from Africa and Asia were included, the majority originated from high-income countries, limiting insights into low-resource contexts. Methodologically, reliance on self-reported measures in some studies introduces recall bias, underscoring the need for objective metrics like device usage tracking. The rapid evolution of digital technologies (e.g., AI-driven platforms) also means findings may not fully capture emerging technologies. Additionally, stringent quality thresholds (e.g., Newcastle–Ottawa Scale scores < 5) prioritized rigor but may have excluded studies with contextual relevance. Finally, despite comprehensive database searches, niche or interdisciplinary sources might have been overlooked. Future research should address these gaps through multilingual inclusion, broader geographic representation, and adaptive methodologies to keep pace with digital technological developments.

## 5 Implications for theory, practice, and future research

### 5.1 Theoretical implications

This review’s findings necessitate refining Cognitive Load Theory, Multimedia Learning Theory, the Document Literacy Framework, and Neuroplasticity Models to account for the context-dependent bidirectional effects of digital technologies on cognition. For instance, action video games enhance perceptual skills and task-switching efficiency [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR10 "Bediou B, Adams DM, Mayer RE, Tipton E, Green CS, Bavelier D. Meta-analysis of action video game impact on perceptual, attentional, and cognitive skills. Psychol Bull. 2018;144(1):77–110. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000130
                  
                .")], aligning with neuroplasticity’s emphasis on skill-based neural adaptation [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR19 "Doidge N. The brain that changes itself: stories of personal triumph from the frontiers of brain science. New York: Viking Press, 2007.")]), yet contribute to cognitive overload when used excessively [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR9 "Shanmugasundaram K, Lee J, Smith T. Excessive smartphone use and reduced attention span in adolescents: a longitudinal study. J Adolesc. 2023;94:102–15. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.adolescence.2023.02.007
                  
                .")], echoing Cognitive Load Theory’s warnings about excessive cognitive demands. Similarly, poorly designed multimedia interfaces overwhelm working memory [[21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR21 "Mayer RE. Multimedia learning. In: Ross BH, editor. Psychology of learning and motivation. San Diego, CA: Academic Press; 2002. p. 85–139.")], while complex electronic texts, such as hypertexts, increase cognitive overload by demanding navigational skills [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR22 "Route JF. The skills of document use: from text comprehension to web-based learning. London, New York: Routledge, 2006.")]. Existing theories do not fully address how a single digital technology produces opposing outcomes based on dose, design, or user intentionality across attention, memory, decision-making, and neuroplasticity. To address this gap, Cognitive Load Theory could integrate a dose–response frame work to explain why moderate, skill-focused digital engagement (e.g., educational apps) reduces cognitive overload, while prolonged, unfocused use depletes working memory [[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR20 "Sweller J. Cognitive load during problem solving: effects on learning. Cogn Sci. 1988;12(2):257–85. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog1202_4
                  
                .")]. Multimedia Learning Theory suggests incorporating design principles, such as coherence and signaling, to predict when digital technologies enhance learning by optimizing dual channel processing or exacerbate overload through cluttered interfaces [[21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR21 "Mayer RE. Multimedia learning. In: Ross BH, editor. Psychology of learning and motivation. San Diego, CA: Academic Press; 2002. p. 85–139.")]. The Document Literacy Framework proposes adding navigational and evaluative skill mediators to account for how strategic processing of electronic texts supports decision-making and memory integration, while poor navigation increases cognitive overload [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR22 "Route JF. The skills of document use: from text comprehension to web-based learning. London, New York: Routledge, 2006.")]. Neuroplasticity Models could incorporate contextual mediators (e.g., goal-directed engagement vs. passive consumption) to predict whether digital technologies foster adaptive plasticity or maladaptive habits [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR19 "Doidge N. The brain that changes itself: stories of personal triumph from the frontiers of brain science. New York: Viking Press, 2007.")]. These refinements support a unified framework, the Cognitive-Multimedia-Document Neuroplasticity (CMDN) Threshold Model, where cognitive outcomes depend on balancing cognitive demands (Cognitive Load Theory), multimedia processing efficiency (Multimedia Learning Theory), navigational and evaluative skills (Document Literacy Framework), and opportunities for structured neural growth (Neuroplasticity Models). For example, metacognitive apps reduce cognitive overload while enhancing self-regulation [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR11 "Greene JA, Copeland DZ, Yu SB. Digital tools and metacognitive awareness in learning: a longitudinal study. Educ Psychol Rev. 2019;31(4):987–1012. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09485-1
                  
                .")], demonstrating synergy between cognitive load reduction and multimedia design, while strategic navigation of digital texts supports memory and decision-making [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR22 "Route JF. The skills of document use: from text comprehension to web-based learning. London, New York: Routledge, 2006.")]. This model moves beyond static “good vs. bad” paradigms to dynamic, context-sensitive explanations of digital technologies’ cognitive impacts.

### 5.2 Practical implications

For educators, policymakers, and practitioners, the findings underscore the urgency of promoting digital literacy and mindful engagement with digital technologies, guided by Cognitive Load Theory, Multimedia Learning Theory, the Document Literacy Framework, and Neuroplasticity Models. These frameworks inform strategies to optimize cognitive outcomes across attention, memory, decision-making, and neuroplasticity while mitigating risks like cognitive overload, as outlined below:

Curriculum Design: Educators should integrate distraction-minimized educational tools, such as apps with metacognitive prompts, to reduce extraneous cognitive load and enhance self-regulated learning. These efforts leverage neuroplasticity to foster cognitive adaptability in underserved populations [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44202-025-00527-0#ref-CR19 "Doidge N. The brain that changes itself: stories of personal triumph from the frontiers of brain science. New York: Viking Press, 2007.")].

### 5.3 Future research directions

To address gaps identified in this review, future studies should:

1.   1.
Expand Geographic and Linguistic Scope: Include non-English studies and underrepresented regions to enhance cross-cultural validity.

2.   2.

3.   3.

For instance, AI’s ability to automate tasks could exacerbate cognitive offloading or reshape neuroplasticity through hyper-personalized stimuli. Early evidence suggests AI may uniquely influence attention (e.g., fragmented focus from chatbot interruptions) and decision-making (e.g., trust in biased recommendations). However, these impacts remain speculative without rigorous study.

4.   4.

args.summary:
This article is a systematic review published in Discover Psychology (December 2025) examining the dual cognitive effects of digital technology engagement across four domains: attention, memory, decision-making, and neuroplasticity. The review synthesizes 15 methodologically rigorous peer-reviewed studies (2017–2023) identified under PRISMA 2020 protocols, framed by Cognitive Load Theory, Multimedia Learning Theory, Neuroplasticity Models, and the Document Literacy Framework.

Key findings include:
- **Attention**: Digital multitasking (smartphones, social media) fragments attention and reduces sustained focus, especially in adolescents. However, action video games enhance perceptual accuracy and task-switching speed.
- **Memory**: Educational apps support metacognitive awareness, while over-reliance on digital tools for information storage reduces intrinsic memory and autobiographical recall.
- **Decision-making**: Real-time digital information improves analytical decision-making in some contexts, but data saturation and algorithm-driven environments promote heuristic shortcuts, undermining critical thinking.
- **Neuroplasticity**: Structured interventions like video game training enhance cognitive control (especially in older adults), while excessive addictive use is linked to structural brain changes and diminished impulse control.

The review proposes a unified Cognitive-Multimedia-Document Neuroplasticity (CMDN) Threshold Model, arguing that cognitive outcomes depend on balancing cognitive demands, multimedia processing efficiency, navigational skills, and opportunities for structured neural growth. Practical implications include curriculum design using distraction-minimized tools, equitable access to cognitive-enhancing technologies, and digital literacy programs. Future research should expand geographic/linguistic scope, incorporate objective usage metrics, and investigate AI-driven technologies.

# Managing cognitive load optimises learning

Implications for policymakers

This explainer gives a brief introduction to cognitive load, focusing on ways to manage it for effective and efficient learning.

Downloads

[Download explainer PDF, 575.54 KB](/sites/default/files/2023-11/managing-cognitive-load-optimises-learning-aa.pdf)

## What is cognitive overload?

Cognitive overload refers to a state that can happen during learning where students struggle to process and store new information in memory. Teaching that actively manages cognitive load has a positive impact on students’ ability to engage with learning tasks and, more importantly, to retain what they have learned as part of those tasks. Cognitive load affects all learners, in all contexts, but can be managed with effective teaching approaches to optimise achievement and outcomes of learning.

This explainer provides a brief introduction to cognitive load, focusing on ways to manage it for effective and efficient learning. Related explainers with similar implications for effective teaching practices and related policies introduce the role of knowledge in the learning process and the positive impact of explicit instruction.

## Role of memory in learning

Students learn by using working memory to focus on and process new information, allowing them to connect it to what they already know. Under the right conditions, new information – whether factual, conceptual or procedural – is transferred to long-term memory, where it is stored as mental models that reflect our understanding of the area of learning. Building on the connections within and between these mental models helps students develop a deeper understanding of an area of learning over time. Knowledge stored in long-term memory can be recalled to working memory, where it can be combined and recombined with other new or remembered information to help students generate novel ideas, solve unfamiliar problems and think critically and creatively (Fiorella & Mayer, 2016; Kirschner et al., 2006).

## Why managing the load on memory is important

Working memory and long-term memory both play important roles in learning, but they operate in different ways. Working memory is a fast and flexible, but unstable, system that can manipulate information quickly, allowing us to use it at a given time without storing information. Novice learners can experience cognitive overload and have trouble retaining and recalling their learning when the limits of working memory are exceeded. Students may experience cognitive overload when processing too much information at one time, when information is very complex, or when trying to learn in overly distracting learning environments. Long-term memory has vast storage capacity, but to use it most effectively, information needs to be transferred between working and long-term memory bit by bit, and retrieved at regular intervals for more secure storage over time.

Working memory is always limited (Craik & Lockhart, 1972; Kirschner & Hendrick, 2020), and some students will experience additional limitations in using working memory, and in processing information (Melby-Lervåg et al., 2016). This makes the management of cognitive load important both for equitable access to educational opportunity, and for supporting excellence in learning achievement.

## Promoting the management of cognitive load for optimal learning

The evidence about how students learn provides a clear direction for the development of curriculum, instructional materials, practice guidance and policies that support effective pedagogical approaches. Without consistent and coherent guidance, schools and teachers are influenced by a range of approaches that may not be based on strong evidence.

Learning is optimised when policy and guidance promotes and supports the following practices:

### Provide small amount of new information to support retention

Teaching that manages cognitive load begins with a clear explanation of what students are expected to learn, and new material is broken up into small, manageable chunks with well-defined goals (Rosenshine, 2012). Information required to complete each learning task is presented in one place and at one time. Information not directly related to the task is excluded to prevent occupying limited space in working memory (Sweller et al., 1998).

### Guide and support learning to help students focus on the essential new information

Students can experience cognitive overload when the task is too conceptually difficult for their current level of knowledge and skills (Centre for Education Statistics and Evaluation [CESE], 2017). Scaffolding is where teachers provide students with more guidance in completing difficult tasks when the students are new to the procedures or concepts being learnt (Rosenshine, 2012). Scaffolds can include models to represent concepts, worked examples to demonstrate the process and goal of completing a task, as well as prompts, information organisers, checklists, and access to reference materials. Scaffolds can be gradually removed as students develop greater proficiency (Perry et al., 2021). Sequencing content logically from simple to complex and providing concrete examples of abstract content can also help limit complexity that may otherwise contribute to cognitive load.

### Draw on prior knowledge and connect new information gradually to optimise the limitations of working memory

Presenting new information gradually so students can store and then retrieve information from long-term memory as they expand on their learning is one of the ways teachers reduce the burden on working memory. A student might initially need nearly all their working memory (several chunks) to represent the idea of an atom, leaving no further room to learn about related topics like an atom’s structure or properties. However, once learned and accessed from long-term memory, the complex idea of the atom will only take up one chunk, leaving the rest of their working memory free to build on that knowledge.

### Prevent misconceptions by checking for understanding throughout learning

Long-term memories are somewhat stable and tend to be recalled or retrieved in the same way they were transferred from working memory. This makes it important to identify and address misunderstandings as they develop, before they are stored in long-term memory. When teachers sequence the information in learning tasks logically, check for understanding frequently, and structure tasks to prevent and correct common errors or misconceptions, they can help students transfer accurate information to long-term memory, avoid misconceptions being formed, and connect their learning meaningfully for deeper understanding of the learning area (Rosenshine, 2012).

### Space learning to allow working memory to rest, and prompt retrieval to allow long-term memory to strengthen

Teachers can support students’ ability to retain and apply learning with spaced and varied opportunities to retrieve, review and practise what they’ve learned. Spacing out learning and providing breaks can account for the increasing limitations of working memory that follow a period of focused effort. When prompted to retrieve what they’ve learned from memory after a break, students form stronger connections in memory. By practising in varied ways, new and unique connections in memory are formed, making it easier to recall relevant knowledge when prompted by a wider range of possible applications in the future (Perry et al., 2021; Rosenshine, 2012).

### Avoid unstructured, student-led approaches for novice learners

School-aged students are regularly required to learn new information and can be considered novices at that point in their learning. The brain of a novice processes information differently from the brain of an expert, even when they are exposed to the same information. Novice learners need more time and guidance than experts because novices first need to build the mental models of understanding in long-term memory that experts already have (Kalyuga, 2007). Learning tasks that are not well-structured and guided expose students to information not directly relevant to the task at hand, which can overload working memory (Sweller, 2016).

When novices receive minimal guidance to complete a new task, their attention may be focused on the process of completing the task and not on thinking about the new information they need to learn within the task. Students may finish tasks without actually connecting and transferring information within the task to long-term memory (CESE, 2017). The high cognitive load associated with minimally guided tasks can lead to gaps in learning and misconceptions that need to be corrected. For example, students asked to collate information to create a slide presentation on an unfamiliar topic, without specific structure and guidance, may later struggle to remember what they found when asked to recall and use the information, because their attention was focused more on the process of developing slides. Once students have mastered the relevant background knowledge of a subject, they can apply and extend their learning effectively through increasingly independent tasks and structured inquiry (Fiorella & Mayer, 2016; Hattie, 2023; Martin & Evans, 2018).

#### Provide a learning-focused environment to prevent distractions that contribute to cognitive load

Visual and auditory distractions may occupy the mental space of students’ working memory that they need to focus on learning content. Additionally, learning environments with unclear behavioural expectations and inconsistent rules and routines can pull students’ focus away from their learning (Alter & Haydon, 2017). Students who have learned the behaviours and routines that are expected of them to the point they become unconscious and automatic won’t have to think about these things while focused on learning. With their focus on learning, this aids effective transfer and retention in long-term memory (Chaffee et al., 2017; Simonsen et al., 2008).

## Implications for policymakers

* When students experience cognitive overload they have difficulty processing, retaining, recalling and applying their learning.
* Unstructured, self-led learning is ineffective for school students encountering new information because they need guidance to master the relevant background knowledge of a subject before they can engage effectively in independent practice.
* Policies and programs that advocate for well-sequenced, spaced explicit instruction and learning-focused environments can facilitate improved learning outcomes.

This explainer from the Australian Education Research Organisation (AERO) introduces cognitive load theory and its implications for optimizing learning, with a focus on policymaker guidance.

**Key concepts:**
- Cognitive overload occurs when students struggle to process and store new information because working memory limits are exceeded
- Working memory is limited and unstable; long-term memory has vast capacity but information must be transferred bit by bit
- Novice learners process information differently from experts and need more guidance

**Practices that optimize learning by managing cognitive load:**
1. Provide small amounts of new information, broken into manageable chunks
2. Guide and support learning through scaffolding (worked examples, models, prompts, checklists)
3. Draw on prior knowledge and connect new information gradually
4. Prevent misconceptions by checking for understanding throughout learning
5. Space learning with breaks and prompt retrieval to strengthen long-term memory
6. Avoid unstructured, student-led approaches for novice learners (minimally guided tasks can overload working memory)
7. Provide learning-focused environments free from distractions and with clear behavioral expectations

**Implications for policymakers:**
- Cognitive overload hinders processing, retention, recall, and application of learning

--- SOURCE 2: Screen Time and Child Development ---
URL: https://www.structural-learning.com/post/screen-time-child-development-teachers-guide

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Screen Time and Child Development: A Teacher's Guide

This article from Structural Learning (published March 27, 2026, updated August 15, 2026) provides evidence-based guidance on screen time and child development, covering digital media effects, age limits, and strategies for teaching healthy tech habits. It draws heavily on the UK's Early Years Screen Time Advisory Group (EYSTAG) independent report and the "Best Start in Life" guidance published in March 2026.

### Key Framework: The Displacement Hypothesis

The central argument is that screen time harms development primarily by **replacing** vital activities (peer play, physical activity, sleep, adult conversation) rather than acting as a direct toxin. What matters is not the screen itself, but **what it replaces, how it is used, and whether an adult is present.**

### Three Main Mechanisms Affecting Development

1. **Joint Attention and Language:** Parental smartphone use ("technoference") disrupts parent-child brain synchrony and reduces conversational turns, which are critical for language acquisition.
2. **Executive Function:** Excessive screen time is associated with poorer attention, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility. Executive function predicts academic achievement more reliably than IQ (Diamond, 2013).
3. **Sensorimotor Development:** Touchscreens offer little proprioceptive/haptic feedback. 28% of reception children attempt to "swipe" book pages as if they were devices.

### Evidence-Based Recommendations by Age

| Age Group | Recommendation |
|-----------|----------------|
| **Under 2** | Avoid screen time except for shared activities (video calls, looking at photos together). Average screen time at 9 months: 29 min/day; by age 2: 127 min/day. Children in lowest income quintile had nearly double the screen time (179 vs 97 min/day). |
| **Ages 2-5** | Maximum 1 hour/day, in short chunks of 30 minutes or less. Slow-paced, predictable content with adult interaction is preferred. Harms accelerate after ~1.5 hours/day at age 2. |
| **School-Age (5-11)** | Screen time competes with homework, reading, physical activity, and socialising. Smartphone use linked with higher impulsivity and lower cognitive flexibility. |
| **Adolescents** | Each additional hour of screen time linked with 3-8 fewer minutes of sleep per night (Przybylski, 2019). |

### Co-Viewing: The Critical Factor

A meta-analysis of 100 studies (Santos et al., 2024) found that **watching alone** is linked with poorer cognitive outcomes, while **co-viewing with an engaged adult** is linked with better outcomes. The adult conversation is the "active ingredient." Co-viewing is most protective for children from deprived backgrounds, who may have the least chance to experience it.

### Content Type Matters

Fast-paced content (frequent scene cuts, rapid speech, complex narratives) should be avoided. Slow-paced, repetitive content with simple backgrounds and clear single narrators is preferred. The "video deficit" means young children learn less from screens than from real-life interaction, a gap that may last until school age.

### What Teachers Can Do

1. **Build Conversational Capacity:** Use structured oracy activities (Think-Pair-Share, Kagan structures) to compensate for displaced home dialogue.
2. **Rebuild Attention Gradually:** Build sustained attention through graduated challenge (5 min → 7 min → 10 min of focused work).
3. **Use Screens Purposefully:** Ask: Could this learning happen without a screen? Am I present and engaged while learners use this screen?
4. **Communicate With Parents:** The message is not "ban screens" but "add shared activities." Co-viewing and discussing content is developmentally beneficial.
5. **Prioritise SEND Considerations:** Screen-based assistive technologies are essential for many learners; time limits should not apply in the same way.

### Key Statistics

- 52% of UK primary staff report worsening school readiness linked to excessive screen exposure at home (Kindred Squared, 2025)
- 28% of reception children try to swipe or tap book pages
- 19% of 3-5 year olds have their own phone
- 91% of 3-5 year olds use video platforms
- Children who met the 1-hour guideline had 3.48 times the odds of better working memory (Carson et al., 2022)
- Co-viewing children were 8.56 times less likely to develop excessive screen habits (Fajardo et al., 2023)

### AI and Emerging Technology

The EYSTAG panel found no convincing evidence on the impact or safety of AI chatbots or AI-enabled toys for children under five. Parents should not let young children use AI tools, toys, or chatbots until the evidence improves.
</summary>

## Summary: What Screen Time Actually Does to Kids According to Research

This in-depth article from ReachLink (published August 6, 2026) examines the research on screen time's effects on children, arguing that the panic often outpaces the science. The core thesis is that the effects of screen time depend far more on content type, age, and parental co-viewing than on daily hours alone.

### Key Methodological Problems
- "Screen time" as a research category lumps together fundamentally different activities (background TV, video chatting, educational apps, passive scrolling), yet most studies treat it as a single daily-hours variable.
- Researchers Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski demonstrated that "researcher degrees of freedom" (small analytical decisions) can produce wildly different conclusions from the exact same dataset.
- Parent-reported screen time estimates are consistently off by 1.5 to 2 hours per day compared to objective tracking.

### Effect Size Comparisons
- Screen time's correlation with language development is approximately r = −0.14, accounting for about **2% of the variance**.
- Reading aloud to children (r ≈ 0.34) explains about 12% of variance — roughly **2.5 times more powerful** than screen time is harmful.
- Poverty's effect on cognitive development (r ≈ 0.30–0.50) dwarfs screen time by a wide margin.

### Key Findings by Age and Content Type
- **Under 18 months**: Strongest case for caution. The "video deficit effect" means babies cannot effectively learn from screens. Screens displace serve-and-return caregiver interaction.
- **Ages 2–5**: AAP's 1-hour daily limit is a cautious extrapolation with a thinner evidence base than commonly assumed. Educational content like Sesame Street shows modest vocabulary gains.
- **Ages 6–12**: Moderate screen use shows minimal negative associations. Content and context matter far more than raw duration.
- **Adolescents**: Primary concerns are social media effects on self-image, sleep disruption from evening device use, and cyberbullying.

### Types of Screen Use and Risk Profiles
1. **Background TV** — Most consistently problematic; reduces parent-child conversation and fragments attention even when no one is actively watching.
2. **Passive streaming alone** — Risk is highest for children under 3; limited concerns for older children watching age-appropriate content.
3. **Educational co-viewing** — Shifts research toward neutral or positive outcomes; parental involvement is the active ingredient.
4. **Video chat** — No negative associations at any age; supports real relationships.
5. **Interactive apps/games** — Mixed evidence; most marketed "educational" apps lack research backing.
6. **Content creation** — Early research suggests this may support development rather than hinder it.

### Evidence-Based Strategies
- Focus on quality, co-viewing, and context over rigid time limits.
- Eliminate background TV during play, meals, and family conversations.
- Protect sleep: screen-free bedrooms and no devices in the hour before bedtime.
- Model intentional screen habits (avoid "parental technoference").

### Where the Evidence is Strongest vs. Weakest
- **Strongest**: Background TV disrupts interaction; passive video under 2 displaces language-building time; screens that crowd out sleep create measurable harm; violent content is associated with increased aggression.
- **Weakest**: Little rigorous support for claims that typical screen use causes brain damage, that young children can develop clinical addiction to screens, or that any exposure leaves lasting developmental harm.

The article concludes that parental warmth, reading aloud, sleep quality, and socioeconomic stability all carry substantially larger effect sizes on child development than screen time does.

--- SOURCE 14: Co-Viewing - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/co-viewing

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This ScienceDirect topic page on 'Co-Viewing' within Psychology comprehensively defines and explores the concept of co-viewing, defined as when an adult watches a television program with a child (Palmer & Sullivan, 2008). It presents co-viewing as a critical form of parental mediation that significantly influences children's learning and development from screen media. 

Key findings from multiple studies and chapters include:
- Co-viewing is not monolithic; it ranges from passive presence to highly active, dialogic engagement. Even low levels can have positive benefits (Uhls & Robb, 2017).
- Three key mechanisms by which active co-viewing supports learning: (1) directing children's attention to the screen, (2) providing cognitive support (e.g., connecting screen content to real life), and (3) offering social feedback (Strouse et al., 2013).
- Dialogic questioning (pausing to ask questions, encourage participation) is more effective for learning than merely directing attention or passive co-viewing. A study of 3-year-olds found dialogic questioning by parents led to superior story comprehension and vocabulary compared to directed attention or control groups (Strouse et al., 2013).
- Parental scaffolding, such as labeling objects or explicitly connecting 2D images to 3D objects, helps children encode information and overcome the 'video deficit' or 'transfer deficit' (learning less from video than live interaction) (Courage & Frizzell, 2020; Strouse & Troseth, 2014).
- The presence of an adult co-viewer provides social contingency and responsiveness that is difficult to replicate with on-screen characters alone, though on-screen prompts or dialogic characters can offer some benefit (Uhls & Robb, 2017; Strouse et al., 2013).
- However, parent-child interactions during co-viewing are often less rich than during reading or play, and co-viewing can sometimes reduce the quantity of parental language (Nathanson & Rasmussen, 2011; Lavigne et al., 2015).
- Research on emotional co-experiencing suggests co-viewing with a close partner can amplify emotional reactions (Clark et al., 2017).
- The page notes that while co-viewing is beneficial, actual parental involvement is inconsistent. Parents report co-viewing only about half the time, and children's media access in bedrooms has diminished opportunities for joint viewing (Courage & Frizzell, 2020; Palmer & Sullivan, 2008).
- The content also distinguishes between 'foreground' media (child-directed) and 'background' media (incidental exposure), noting that background exposure can have negative effects (Pempek & Lauricella, 2017).
</summary>

Co-viewing is when an adult watches a television program with a child (Palmer & Sullivan, 2008). Active co-viewing supports young children's learning from video through three mechanisms: directing attention, supporting cognition, and social feedback (Strouse et al., 2013). Even low levels of co-viewing can have positive benefits (Uhls & Robb, 2017). Children whose parents engaged in dialogic questioning while co-watching videos outscored other groups on story comprehension and vocabulary (Strouse et al., 2013). Parent-child interactions during co-viewing are not always as engaging or as rich as they are during other common activities (Nathanson & Rasmussen, 2011).

The study was conducted by researchers from Texas Tech University, Michigan State University, and other institutions.

The WHO recently updated screen time guidelines, recommending no more than one hour per day for children aged 2-4 and no screen time for children under 1 year, citing risks of obesity, poor school performance, and other problems.

The study had three goals: (1) compare content-level and message-level effects of co-viewing; (2) investigate cognitive responses to three types of information commonly used in children's programming (plot explicit, educational explicit, and implicit inference); and (3) explore how co-viewing affects children's cognitive processing of these information types.

**Method:** Participants were 6-13 years old (mean ~9 years). Parent-child groups watched one of two 11-minute clips from educational programs (Man vs. Wild - High Arousal; Pure Nature - Low Arousal) in four conditions: high/low arousing content with/without parent. Children's heart rates were monitored via electrodes as a measure of cognitive resource allocation.

**Results:** Co-viewing affected overall message processing and initial heart rate. Plot explicit content produced the greatest resource allocation. Educational explicit and inferential implicit information caused small cardiac accelerations. Co-viewing led to more encoding when content was exciting and plot-related, but less encoding when content was boring.

**Implications:** Parents should be aware that their presence during television consumption affects encoding. Content creators should tie educational content closely to storylines. The researchers call for further research on external vs. internal stimuli effects on children's learning and behavior.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 25: Parenting to Reduce Child Screen Time: A Feasibility Pilot Study ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5747554

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed feasibility pilot study published in the Journal of Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics (2018) examining a novel one-session intervention designed to help parents reduce their child's screen time.

**Objective:** To examine the feasibility and preliminary outcomes of a one-session parent intervention combining didactics and hands-on assistance to reduce child screen time.

**Method:** 39 parents of children aged 5-12 years were randomized to either the intervention (a two-hour workshop: one-hour instructional period on technology-specific parenting + one-hour hands-on workshop) or a wait-list control group. The intervention covered psychoeducation on media effects, parenting strategies (setting boundaries, positive reinforcement), and practical guidance on setting parental controls and passwords on devices. Outcomes measured included technology-specific parenting strategies, parent appraisal of daily screen time, daily diary reports, and parent satisfaction.

**Results:**
- Recruitment: 52 parents screened, 39 (75%) randomized over 6 weeks at a cost of $2,848.11.
- Retention: 82% completed the 6-week post-assessment (85% intervention, 77% waitlist).
- Fidelity: 100% of intervention components were covered, with 98.8% rated as "covered well"; observer agreement was 97%+.
- Preliminary outcomes: The intervention group showed medium-to-large within-group effect sizes for technology-specific parenting (d=.76) and parent appraisal of screen time (d=.51), compared to smaller effects in the waitlist group (d=.52 and .26 respectively). Between-group effect sizes were in the medium range for both measures.
- Daily diary screen time did not change significantly for either group.
- Parent satisfaction was high (ratings between 4.0-5.0 on a 5-point scale), and 95% of parents reported implementing or being likely to implement the skills learned.

**Conclusions:** The intervention showed promise as a brief, feasible approach to reducing child screen time. The study highlights the importance of assessment methods (parent appraisal vs. daily diaries) and the need for a full-scale evaluation. The intervention is notable for its brevity, flexibility to incorporate all media devices, and combination of didactic teaching with hands-on assistance.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: How Can We Help Kids With Self-Regulation? ---
URL: https://childmind.org/article/can-help-kids-self-regulation

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The article from Child Mind Institute addresses how to help children with self-regulation—the ability to manage emotions and behavior according to situational demands. It notes that frequent meltdowns in children over age five may indicate problems with self-regulation, which is common in children with ADHD or anxiety.

Key points include:
- **Self-regulation** involves resisting highly emotional reactions, calming oneself, adjusting to changes, and handling frustration without outbursts.
- **Emotional dysregulation** can manifest as immediate strong reactions or a slow buildup leading to outbursts.
- **Causes** include temperament and learned behavior; when parents consistently soothe children, kids may "outsource" self-regulation as a habit.
- **Teaching strategies** include "scaffolding"—coaching children through difficult situations with support, then gradually reducing assistance. Techniques include practicing transitions (e.g., stopping video games), dry runs (e.g., short store visits), and breaking tasks into small steps with positive reinforcement.
- **Approaches**: Mindfulness, parent training programs, and dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) for older kids are recommended. Experts emphasize slowing down, modeling self-reflection, and providing non-judgmental feedback.
- **Key quote**: "The family environment is the most important piece" (Dr. Matthew Rouse).

Clinical experts cited: Matthew H. Rouse, PhD, and Alnardo Martinez, LMHC.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Self-regulation is the ability to manage your emotions and behavior in accordance with the demands of the situation." (Matthew Rouse, PhD), "Some kids are instantaneous — they have a huge, strong reaction... They can't inhibit that immediate behavior response." (Matthew Rouse, PhD), "We approach self-regulation skills in the same way we approach other skills, academic or social: isolate that skill and provide practice." (Scott Bezsylko), "When kids are part of an environment that's reflective and analytic as opposed to emotional and fast-paced, they can learn to make better choices." (Scott Bezsylko), "It seems to me that the family environment is the most important piece." (Matthew Rouse, PhD)

The guide is organized into key sections covering cognitive development, social-emotional health, physical health, and practical parenting tips.

**Key Topics Covered:**

**Big Do's and Don'ts:** Set consistent rules around media use, help build self-regulation skills without screens, gradually increase media privileges based on demonstrated responsibility, delay smartphones as long as possible, support sleep quality, discourage offloading cognitive tasks to AI, minimize background TV, encourage print-based reading, model healthy media use, watch for problematic media use, discuss family values, and develop critical thinking skills.

**Cognitive Development & Learning:** Executive function skills (working memory, organization, time management) are crucial for this age group. Quality sleep is foundational for brain development. Building focus and concentration requires sustained attention activities. Background TV predicts less focused attention. Print-based reading engages brain networks better than digital reading. AI tools like ChatGPT should not be used for foundational learning tasks (users must be 13+). Multitasking prevents deep cognitive processing. Maintaining a healthy dopamine balance between high-stimulation activities (video games, TikTok) and low-stimulation activities (homework, exercise) is important. Problematic media use is associated with structural brain changes mimicking adult addictions. Screen time may displace activities better for cognitive development like board games, creative expression, and imaginative play.

**Social-Emotional Health:** Prioritize in-person relationship time. Give children non-screen tools for self-regulation. Parents should model personal social connection and reduce "technoference" (device use during parent-child time). Support self-esteem by focusing on internal qualities rather than external appearance. Foster social belonging. Avoid violent media exposure (linked to aggression, fear, desensitization). Wait on social media and messaging platforms (most have age 13+ restrictions). Over 92% of 5th graders have been exposed to hate speech on social media in the last month. Build character-forming habits and family culture. Encourage helping behaviors at home.

**Practical Tips:** Use the "Living Your Life Out Loud" technique (narrating your own screen use). Use hard copies of homework. Viewing content repetitively helps learning. --- SOURCE 3: Screen time and preschool children: Promoting health and ... ---
URL: https://cps.ca/en/documents/position/screen-time-and-preschool-children

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Screen Time and Preschool Children: Promoting Health and Development in a Digital World

**Source:** Canadian Paediatric Society (CPS) Position Statement  
**Posted:** November 24, 2022  
**Principal Author:** Michelle Ponti MD, CPS Digital Health Task Force  
**Published in:** Paediatr Child Health 2023;28(3):184–192

### Background
This is an updated statement (replacing the 2017 version) examining the benefits and risks of screen media exposure for children under 5 years, with the COVID-19 pandemic having dramatically transformed family media environments. The guidance is built on four evidence-based principles: **Minimizing, Mitigating, Mindfully using, and Modelling** healthy screen use.

### Key Statistics
- Nearly all Canadian children are exposed to screens by age 2
- Only 15% of Canadian children aged 3-4 meet screen time guidelines of <1 hour/day
- Pre-pandemic, average parent-reported screen time for this age group was 1.9 hours/day
- In the U.S., 9 of 10 children are introduced to a device before their first birthday

### Developmental Impacts
- **No established benefits** of media exposure for infants and toddlers, except for interactive video-chatting
- Children under 2 cannot learn efficiently from screens; they learn best through face-to-face interaction
- Quality screen media (educational, age-appropriate, co-viewed with adults) can benefit children aged 2-5
- Language delay is a closely studied correlate: greater screen use in infancy is associated with lower language skills at 3-4 years
- Background TV negatively affects language development, cognitive development, and executive function skills
- Prolonged screen exposure reduces opportunities for optimal development

### Psychosocial Impacts
- Quality content can enhance social skills, especially for disadvantaged children
- "Technoference" (interruption of interactions by digital devices) is an emerging risk factor
- Higher screen time in preschoolers is linked to increased externalizing behaviours, lower self-regulation, and reduced executive function
- Using screens to calm or distract children may lead to overdependence on screens for emotion regulation

### Physical Health Impacts
- Screen time is associated with adiposity, motor development, cognitive development, and psychosocial health
- Risk of myopia increases with more screen time and less outdoor time
- Screen time before bedtime is associated with sleep problems (less sleep, later bedtimes, delayed sleep onset)
- Commercial TV exposes children to advertisements for unhealthy foods

### Key Recommendations for Families

**Minimize screen time:**
- No screen time for children under 2 (except video-chatting)
- Children 2-5: Limit to about 1 hour or less per day
- Avoid screens at least 1 hour before bedtime
- Maintain screen-free times, especially for family meals and book-sharing

**Mitigate risks:**
- Co-view with children whenever possible
- Prioritize educational, age-appropriate, interactive content
- Support self-regulation skills without relying on screens
- Limit exposure to advertising and commercialized content

**Be mindful:**
- Develop a family media plan for when, how, and where screens may be used
- Prioritize shared family media use over solitary use
- Encourage older siblings to mentor younger children's digital encounters

**Model healthy screen use:**
- Participate in activities unrelated to screens (reading, outdoor play, board games, crafts)
- Turn off devices during family time
- Avoid background TV
- Advocate for healthier screen use policies in child care and schools
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: Teaching self-control: Evidence-based tips ---
URL: https://parentingscience.com/teaching-self-control

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Parenting Science, authored by Dr. Gwen Dewar (updated November 2023), provides evidence-based guidance on teaching self-control to children. It defines self-control as the ability to regulate oneself—resisting distractions, inhibiting impulses, managing emotions, delaying gratification, and planning ahead. The article notes that while self-control develops naturally between ages 3 and 7, individual variation is significant, and poor self-regulation is linked to lower academic achievement, anxiety, depression, aggression, obesity, and drug dependency. The article presents 14 tips for fostering self-discipline, each supported by research:

1. **Remove temptations** from the environment (out of sight, out of mind).
2. **Create environments that consistently reward self-control**—children's willingness to delay gratification depends on trust that rewards will be delivered (citing Kidd et al. 2011).
3. **Use timely reminders** for young children rather than just giving them time to think (Barker & Munakata 2015).
4. **Play self-regulation games** like modified Red Light/Green Light, freeze games, and orchestra conductor games (Tominey & McClelland 2009; Traverso et al. 2015, 2019).
5. **Give kids breaks**—self-control depletes over time, and downtime helps recharge.
6. **Encourage cooperative pretend play** to build self-regulatory skills (White & Carlson 2021; Thibodeau et al. 2016).
7. **Limit screen time**—excessive screen time is linked to poorer self-regulation, especially in toddlers (McHarg et al. 2020; McMath et al. 2023).
8. **Turn "must-do" tasks into "want-to" tasks** by finding ways to make them enjoyable.
9. **Instill a growth mindset**—praise effort and strategies, not traits (related to Carol Dweck's work).
10. **Develop attention and working memory skills** through evidence-based strategies.
11. **Be an "emotion coach"**—talk about feelings, show empathy, and discuss coping strategies (Shortt et al. 2010).
12. **Encourage planning practice**—teach kids to identify obstacles, use self-talk, and think ahead (Lidstone et al. 2010; Unterrainer et al. 2006).
13. **Handle misbehavior thoughtfully**—avoid both permissive and authoritarian parenting styles; corporal punishment may harm self-regulation development.
14. **Respect children's need for autonomy**—kids are more likely to cooperate when they perceive adult authority as legitimate.

The article concludes with additional resources and an extensive reference list of academic studies.
</summary>

Contrary to expectations that higher-SES families would adhere more closely to pediatric guidelines, quantitative analyses of nationally representative PSID Child Development Supplement data (N=427, 2014) found that higher-SES children used technology as frequently as lower-SES children and far exceeded AAP recommendations. However, there were class differences: higher-SES children spent less time watching TV (11.83 vs. 17.53 hrs/week for high school diploma families) but more time on non-TV technology (16.19 vs. 11.96 hrs/week). The study concludes that cultures and structures around children's technology use are in flux, with emerging class-based distinctions around parenting. The research engages with fundamental cause theory, cultural capital theory, and individualist parenting perspectives to explain why higher-SES families did not follow pediatric guidelines for screen time.

The analytic sample included 1,952 teens.

**Key Findings:**
- Approximately 50.4% of teens had 4+ hours of daily non-schoolwork screen time.
- Teens with high screen time were significantly more likely to experience: infrequent physical activity (45.6% vs 32.1%), infrequent strength training (23.0% vs 13.3%), being infrequently well-rested (59.9% vs 40.1%), irregular sleep routine (49.2% vs 29.2%), weight concerns (37.8% vs 25.3%), depression symptoms (25.9% vs 9.5%), anxiety symptoms (27.1% vs 12.3%), infrequent social and emotional support (48.6% vs 35.1%), and insufficient peer support (37.0% vs 30.4%).

**Adjusted Results (controlling for sociodemographics):**
After adjustment, all associations remained significant except for insufficient peer support. Notably, teens with high screen time were 2.51 times more likely to have depression symptoms and 2.12 times more likely to have anxiety symptoms. Other adjusted prevalence ratios included: infrequent physical activity (APR=1.33), infrequent strength training (APR=1.64), infrequently well-rested (APR=1.45), irregular sleep routine (APR=1.58), weight concerns (APR=1.42), and infrequent social/emotional support (APR=1.29).

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review and meta-analysis published in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity (2021) by Jones, Armstrong, Weaver, Parker, von Klinggraeff, and Beets from the University of South Carolina. The study aimed to identify behavior change techniques and study characteristics associated with effectiveness in behavioral interventions to reduce children's (0–18 years) screen time.

**Methods:** A literature search of four databases (Ebscohost, Web of Science, EMBASE, PubMed) was conducted between January/February 2020 and updated in July 2021. The search identified 15,529 articles, with 204 studies ultimately providing quantitative data for the meta-analysis. Information on study characteristics (sample size, duration) and behavior change techniques (e.g., goal-setting, feedback) were extracted. Meta-regressions explored associations between intervention effectiveness and behavior change techniques/study characteristics.

**Results:** The overall random effects summary showed a small, beneficial impact of screen time interventions compared to controls (SDM = 0.116, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.15). Inclusion of the Goals, Feedback, and Planning behavioral techniques cluster was associated with a positive impact on intervention effectiveness (SDM = 0.145, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.18). Interventions with smaller sample sizes (n < 95) delivered over short durations (< 52 weeks) were associated with larger effects. As sample size increased, intervention effectiveness diminished even when Goals, Feedback, and Planning techniques were present. Studies varied considerably in duration (median = 24 weeks), sample size (median = 317, range 6 to 35,157), and quality (67% fair, 27% poor, only 13 good quality). The most frequently included behavior change techniques were information on behavior-health link (k=168), instruction (k=145), and social support (k=134). The Knowledge and Consequences cluster was most common (k=186), while Behavioral Repetition and Practice was least common (k=148).

**Conclusions:** Both intervention content and context are important for designing effective screen time reduction interventions. The Goals, Feedback, and Planning cluster (including goal setting, goal review, self-monitoring) was the driving behavioral strategy associated with enhanced effectiveness. However, effects diminished as interventions were scaled up. Identifying active ingredients will be crucial for optimizing interventions along the translational continuum.

# Screen Time Interventions for Children

## Summary

This webpage from the County Health Rankings & Roadmaps' "What Works for Health" resource provides evidence-based information on screen time interventions for children. These interventions encourage children to spend less time on TV and other stationary screen media (computers, video games) and typically do not address mobile screens (smartphones, tablets). They teach self-management skills using tracking, monitoring, classroom education, counseling, and family/peer support, and can include physical activity and/or healthy diet components.

**Evidence Rating: Scientifically Supported** — The highest rating, indicating the strategy is most likely to make a difference, tested in many robust studies with consistently positive results.

**Disparity Rating: Inconclusive impact on disparities** — Not enough evidence to assess potential impact on disparities.

## Key Findings

### Expected Benefits
- Reduced sedentary screen time
- Increased physical activity
- Improved dietary habits
- Improved weight status

### Potential Benefits
- Improved sleep

### Effectiveness
- Strong evidence that screen time interventions reduce sedentary screen time among children under 14.
- Interventions including nutrition and physical activity components also increase physical activity and improve dietary habits and weight-related outcomes.
- Overall small but significant effects on stationary screen use.
- May be especially effective for children under age 6, but effective up to age 18.
- Benefits children across urban/suburban settings, various socioeconomic/racial/ethnic backgrounds, and weight statuses.

### Key Implementation Factors
- **Family and parental support** significantly increase effectiveness, reducing sedentary behavior and fostering long-term healthy habits.
- More successful with shorter duration (less than a year, sometimes less than 3 months).
- Community or home-based settings are more effective.
- School-based interventions can be incorporated into curricula; teacher training may increase effectiveness.
- Use of Goals, Feedback, and Planning behavioral techniques improves outcomes.
